speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I notice that the next premier of British Columbia, Mr. Laing, is in the gallery.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence with reference to the press report that on his return from Paris he stated that Canada's commitments under NATO have not been altered, but that Canada has joined with other NATO partners in a three-year agreement about building airfields, fuel lines, and other parts of what is called the infrastructure of the western defence system. Can the minister advise the house of the exact situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Greenwood was good enough to give me notice of his question. It is really in two parts. The first refers to my statement that Canada's commitments under NATO have not been altered. Canada's military commitments continue as they have been disclosed to this house and to the country repeatedly. We have fulfilled our undertaking to supply an army brigade group, with the committal of the 27th infantry brigade to the integrated force, in November of 1951.
With regard to the air force, in addition to the wing of three squadrons in Great Britain, we have committed another wing of three squadrons located at Grostenquin in France as from November, 1952. Another wing at Zweibrucken was committed last Sunday, in a ceremony there and a third wing in Europe will be taking its place later this year at Baden-Sollingen. So the strength of the R.C.A.F. in Europe as part of the integrated force will be increased by 200 per cent this year.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The navy position is as described in the white paper and in the debate on the estimates.
With regard to the infrastructure, the position was stated in an official press communique authorized to be issued by the North Atlantic council at its meeting in Paris held on Thursday, April 23. That was, I believe, reported in the Canadian press on the following day. I have seen the Canadian Press dispatch dated from Paris, April 24, which was printed extensively in the Canadian press. The position is as stated in the press communique and reported in the press that the countries have agreed on a three-year program, and Canada's share of that program will be 7.13 per cent.

May I ask a
supplementary question?
Subject to the money being voted by parliament.

I was going to ask that question. The report by Secretary Dulles is that the additional expenditure will be $770 million. The minister has said that our share of that is 7 per cent. What I am still puzzled about is how that squares with the minister's statement that our commitments have not been altered. Did the minister mean that it is not a commitment until the House of Commons votes it? Nevertheless it would still be something to which we would be at least morally committed to some extent.

I think the hon. member is quite right. The government has indicated its intention to ask for this money. If it does not ask for it, then we will not be living up to the commitment of the government. It is the only way we can make international agreements. In the statement I made I was referring particularly to military commitments, to which the member of the press who spoke to me had reference. Infrastructure is a matter that is now dealt with by the Minister of Finance.
Does not the minister think that when making these statements it would be better to make an overall statement? I think the statement that he made is subject to misunderstanding.

The matter was dealt with adequately in the press release and reported in the Canadian press. Supplementary to that, having regard to what I had said about military commitments, I made the statement I did and it is completely correct.

On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister as he may not be present this morning when the agriculture estimates are up. I should like to ask him, in view of his telegram of April 29 to the premier of Saskatchewan in regard to the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project, whether or not, if the government of Saskatchewan limits the expenditures required to be made by the dominion government to whatever limitation the Prime Minister has in mind, the government intends to go ahead. If so, in view of that telegram, what is the limitation of expenditure that the government is prepared to accept and undertake in order to go ahead with this?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the limitation of
expenditure has not been considered in precise figures. This is a very large undertaking which would provide for the generation of power and for the possibility of irrigation that would affect, I think, only two-fifths of one per cent of the agricultural lands of Saskatchewan. In view of the relatively small area that would be affected, the capital cost appears to be very substantial.
The dam would provide a reservoir which would have the twofold purpose of providing water for the development of power and for irrigation. It is something that has to be examined in relation to the benefits that would result from the joint expenditure. This would be an undertaking in which the two governments would be co-operating, but


nevertheless it has to be an undertaking that reasonable men can regard as a proper investment of public funds.
The estimates made by the P.F.R.A. and those contained in the report of the royal commission are so divergent that what we had in mind Was that there should be some effort made to get firm commitments from reliable contractors as to what they would be prepared to do this for. If it were going to cost the amount reported by the royal commission, I think even the hon. member would find it difficult to satisfy himself that it was a wise investment. There are assertions that those estimates are extravagant-I do not know. There are assertions that the estimates made by the P.F.R.A. engineers are altogether insufficient-I do not know whether that is so.
This is a matter where the two governments would be involved. Those governments represent the Canadian people and they have to remember their responsibility to the Canadian people. It is necessary to consider what the total cost of this would be; what power would be developed and what it would be worth when compared with power that could be produced by other methods; what prospects there would be of having this irrigation water used in a really beneficial way.
There is no doubt that irrigation can create a situation where much smaller areas are sufficient to use in a practical and useful way much more labour than is required on similar areas for other forms of agricultural pursuits. Is it likely that this two-fifths of one per cent of the arable land of the province would with irrigation become such that the occupants would want to change to that kind of farming? Neither the government of Saskatchewan nor the government of Canada wants to erect a pyramid in Saskatchewan. If there is an investment made there they want to be satisfied that most people will regard it as a reasonable thing to do for furthering the economic development of that area. The costs are an important factor.
What I had particularly in mind was that there must not be left any impression that the federal government by contributing to this project was subsidizing the development of power. We do not do that in any province; it has not been our policy to assist the provinces in the development of power. There is a divergency of view as to what proportion of the cost of creating that reservoir should be attributed to power development in order to avoid creating the feeling that there was a subsidy to power included in it.

I do not think that it would be fair for us to take the position that the premier of Saskatchewan had assumed we were taking and say, "We will not give any further consideration to this project until you make a definite proposal." We have stated what we think are the principles involved in the proposal and we think that that is something which representatives of the two governments should sit down and discuss. Then we would probably attempt to ascertain if it would be possible to get firm commitments from reliable contractors so that there would be a ceiling on any commitment that the federal government made with respect to its contribution to the project. We do not want to make an open-ended commitment even on a percentage basis because there are such wide discrepancies in the estimates that are made as to what this would cost. I cannot be any more precise than that. We do not want to turn our backs on it but we do say there are certain principles that would have to be implemented in any proposal that we could consider. We are prepared to discuss the whole situation to see if, including these principles in a proposal, it is possible to make this something that will look like a reasonable thing to undertake in the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: I want to thank the Prime Minister for that statement. He has spoken about an open-ended commitment. This would seem to be a commitment open at both ends. May I ask the Prime Minister to what extent, having regard to what the government now knows, the government would be prepared to go in accepting responsibility for expenditure? In other words, what limitation does the government have as to the extent to which it will go in a financial commitment with reference to the matters to be discussed between the provincial government and the federal government? Second, are contractors being asked at the present time for firm commitments to determine how much they are prepared to do the construction work for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
No, there has been no invitation to tender and there will not be any invitation to tender until there has been a discussion and a clearing up of the situation as the result of the discussion between the two governments. The hon. gentleman says:	What limit would the federal government put upon its contribution? I cannot give him that in figures, but I can tell him that it would be along the lines that have been followed in the other major irrigation projects. The only part the federal government would be prepared to consider would
Inquiries of the Ministry be that which related to getting the water there as in the St. Mary and other projects, it being left to the provincial authorities and the irrigation districts to take the water from the reservoir and get it to the lands on which it was to be used. Those are the guiding principles but it is not possible to translate them into actual figures at the present time.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question based on the desirability of the construction of the project beginning this year. By what method, if that is possible, could additional moneys be obtained by the federal government for construction this year? In the details of the estimates there is only an amount totalling $500,000, and I believe the Prime Minister would agree that if construction were to start this year it would take some millions of dollars.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
I do not for a moment envisage a situation where actual construction could be commenced this year. I think that if the two governments agreed that they were going to ask for tenders they would have to provide something for the expenses that would be incurred by contractors making those tenders if after they were submitted it was decided that they were of such an amount that contracts could not be let. You could not expect contractors to make tenders unless they were going to be reimbursed in some way for their work in preparing tenders, or were entitled to expect that one of the tenderers would get a contract, that there had been a firm decision in advance of tenders being submitted that the work would be proceeded with.
What I envisage is that there would have to be tenders or some other way of placing a ceiling upon the federal commitment. If the province of Saskatchewan were in a position to say:	Well, whatever the cost may
be we want it proceeded with and your commitment will be limited to so much, that would be one situation, but I do not anticipate that that is probable. The other would be to make some arrangement whereby serious tenderers could be invited to make their best bids with the prospect that they would not be doing so at a loss if their bids were found to be of such an amount that the project could not be proceeded with now.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this is a matter of general concern and that discussion of it was deferred while we were waiting for the report of the royal commission, can the Prime Minister tell us whether the government has considered the
4646	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry royal commission report, whether it is prepared to accept the recommendations contained therein, and if not, whether it is making other inquiries to determine whether it should be accepted?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
The government has no alternative but to accept the report submitted by the royal commissioners. That is the report that they made. Whether or not that report convinces each member of the government that an undertaking of that magnitude would involve the costs that the report envisages is quite another question. There are many who feel that the estimates contained therein are altogether too high. There are many who feel that the estimates of the P.F.R.A. engineers, with a slight increase, are much more apt to be accurate. But there is such a wide difference there that no one can say that the opinions that have been expressed as to what the cost would be are absolutely accurate.
No one can disregard the fact that the commissioners, who were men of experience, have investigated and have come to the conclusions expressed in their report. The government of Saskatchewan says:	We do
not accept that. There are others besides the government of Saskatchewan who say: We do not accept that; we think that the estimates are quite extravagant. I do not know. I do not think it would be prudent for any government, federal or provincial, to go into the matter until some further way is found of ascertaining just what is going to be involved. It may be that the most practical way would be to devise a scheme whereby serious contractors would be invited to make firm bids under some kind of arrangement whereby, if their bids were such that none of them could be accepted, they would get some compensation for the expenses they had incurred in making those firm bids.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: There is one further question I had intended to ask the Prime Minister. Does he expect to advertise for tenders from contractors in order to ascertain what the costs will be before deciding whether or not to go ahead with the project?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: The Prime Minister does not intend to call for tenders, but the Prime Minister feels that tenders should be called for if there is no other way of placing a ceiling upon what would oe the commitment of the federal government if it entered into the implementation of the project.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
In order to determine
whether to go ahead.
[Mr. Drew.)

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
Whether or not to go
ahead.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is not in the nature of a debate-

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: I am glad to know that.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext: -but after all when a matter of this importance comes forward I think hon. members are entitled to know as clearly as possible what the situation is. As I understand the answer that has just been given by the Prime Minister, it is that in his opinion it would be wise to call for firm tenders so that, as a result of those firm tenders, some estimate might be made of the cost; and this would not be regarded as a step indicating a decision to proceed but rather as a means of obtaining information. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LIMITATIONS ON EXPENDITURE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
quite right. It would be regarded as a means of obtaining information because, for my part, I could not undertake at this time to recommend the amount of expenditure which the royal commission felt would be required to carry out the project.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister? In view of the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), both of whom are reported to have made statements on the St. Lawrence seaway development yesterday, can the Prime Minister say whether there are any changes in government policy with respect to the development of that project which should be communicated to the house? The Prime Minister knows that the Minister of Transport made a statement to the effect that the project might be proceeded with partly by the United States and partly by Canada. The Minister of Resources and Development, on the other hand, said if the United States would just get out of the way Canada would go it alone.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext:
There has been no change in nolicy. It has been the policy of the government, ever since the legislation was introduced into parliament here, to proceed alone if there is not a new arrangement arrived at for carrying it out as a joint undertaking. My understanding is that tne Minister of
Inquiries of the Ministry Transport has declared:	"If you cannot
make arrangements with us nothing will prevent you, if the power development proceeds, from providing a canal on your own side of the boundary. We have undertaken to provide one on our side. If we can agree to co-operate on one canal so much the better; but there is nothing now that would prevent the start of work except the designation of a United States agency to join with the hydro commission of Ontario in proceeding with the power development."

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext:
May I ask a
supplementary question? Would not the Prime Minister consider that if the present proposal, namely to have two canals, were to enter the picture that would so greatly alter the decision that was made by us that it would involve reconsideration?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext: I am not sure that is so. I have been told by competent experts that, just as two canals are required at Sault Ste! Marie, the traffic is apt to be such that it will not be long before two canals are required in the international section of the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext: I would not undertake to offer an opinion on that; but my question to the Prime Minister, 'as a lawyer, was whether he thought that what was decided in this house was a canal on the basis of its being a sole canal rather than a canal which might be built in conjunction with another.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext:
I do not think any
thought was given at that time to the possibility of there being a second canal, and parliament authorized the St. Lawrence authority to proceed either alone or jointly with the United States authorities in providing a seaway. If there were other arrangements made with the United States authorities those arrangements would naturally be brought before parliament for its consideration.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext:
Has the Prime Minister
considered stating a deadline beyond which the patience of Canada will not be extended in this matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. I
think this is something which is bound to be done and we want it done just as early as possible-and we are exerting every effort to have it done just as early as possible.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY FOLLOWING MINISTERIAL COMMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: ELECTRICAL INTERFERENCE WITH RECEPTION AT PORT CHURCHILL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale) asked whether the Department of Transport had received any complaints regarding interference with radio reception at port Churchill and, if so, what steps were being taken to remedy the situation. I have made inquiries and I find that the only complaint received was received some time ago from the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward). Inquiries were made and it has been established that the interference is due not to the military establishment but to conditions in the local townsite. It is hoped that suppressors will be available in a short time to eliminate the interference.

Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the resignation of Arthur Laing, Esquire, as member for the electoral district of Vancouver South.
Accordingly I have issued my warrant to the chief electoral officer to make out a new writ of election for the said electoral district.

speechtext:
What I specifically refer to is whether or not it is intended to proceed with the report we had presented this morning. I would point out that at the time it arose not one of us knew the length of it or


the extent of it, and when it became apparent it was as long as it was we knew then the form of the recommendations. What it is important to know is whether or not there is any thought of introducing the amendments to the Criminal Code at this session.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION TO BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
They are now before the house, Mr. Speaker. The question would be, is there any intention of proceeding with the Criminal Code and these recommended amendments. There has been a large amount of work done, I understand in a very cooperative and helpful fashion, by >the members of this committee representing all groups in this house. This is a most important piece of legislation. It is not a piece of legislation about which there could or should be any diverging views from the standpoint of the political policies of any of the parties in the house. I do not think it is the kind of legislation that should be enacted on majority votes, or that should be pressed as something about which there was a political controversy. I think it would be unfortunate if our Criminal Code came to be regarded as something that had been enacted as the result of majority votes on matters that were the subject of political controversy.
I think everyone having anything to do with the preparation and enactment of the Criminal Code would feel that this was a major service to the Canadian nation generally, and one upon which there may be diverging views with respect to certain points, but not views that were inspired by any partisan political considerations. If when the matter is called it should appear that there may be a divergence of views that would be apt to give the impression that there was a political controversy about this bill, it should not be proceeded with now.' On the other hand I think it would be only fair to the members of the house who have put in so much work in this committee to have the matter come before the house instead of being left over, unless there are serious reasons for doing so.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FURTHER LEGISLATION TO BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I subscribe to the convictions expressed by the Prime Minister that, in a measure of this kind, which constitutes the essential framework of our society so far as the more serious aspects of the conduct of our people may be concerned, whatever differences of opinion there may be should not be differences of political points of view but rather differences as to the way in which this could best be done. That was amply illustrated, and illustrated in a very refreshing manner during the course of the sittings of this committee. It was very interesting to hear appeals to tradition from those

who may have been regarded as the least likely, from a doctrinal point of view, to suggest that idea. It would be extremely interesting to hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) say that, in matters of this kind, he is a conservative.
The fact remains, however, that it is desirable, with such extensive changes and where there is not only the desire to do something but there are also legal considerations of the possible consequences of changes in wording and departures from established legal procedures, that we should have ample time to consider the matter. No one is more interested than I am to see certain amendments made. I have been pressing, for instance, for a much wider provision in the Criminal Code to deal with communism in this country. It is certain that that, in itself, would raise a very extensive discussion. It is quite certain that there would be an extensive discussion concerning certain procedure connected with some aspects of our criminal law, as indicated by the discussion in the committee. A number of recommendations that were made by the committee were the result of majority votes. My information is that those who voted against the adoption of those particular amendments in the committee have reserved their own opinions and reserved also the right to raise these same objections in the House of Commons, where they felt that perhaps their views might receive a different consideration.
Only last night, for instance, there was an extensive discussion concerning the extremely difficult problem of lotteries, and the preposterous situation that now results under the laws we have. This calls for consideration by those who do not like to see on the statute books any laws which are openly broken day by day, and which remain there as an encouragement to a state of mind which might more easily lead to breaking other laws.
We are ready to proceed. We are anxious to have a number of these things dealt with. We wish to leave no doubt, however, that there will be an extensive discussion of a number of these subjects. I have only indicated a few.
From the reading of only one page of the 26 pages of this report, hon. members know the extent of the changes that are proposed, and how confusing some of the wording will be, as well as the consideration that would be required. We are certainly ready to proceed, but if we are going to proceed with this bill, then let us abandon these very exhausting hours that have been instituted for the purpose of expediting the termination of the session. It is quite clear that this is going to call for an extended debate. We are ready,

and we are anxious to deal with it. But if we do so, then let us plan the sittings of this house in a way that recognizes the fact that this is going to introduce an extended debate which would, of course, immediately remove the reasons for the hours that we are now sitting.
