The minister can make his speech. I have the floor. I did not interrupt the minister. The Prime Minister's statement this morning was clear and unequivocal. It was this:	We do not know what
the cost is going to be; we have not accepted the findings of the royal commission; we have no evidence yet as to whether those findings are correct; we do not know exactly the course we are going to follow; we have in mind the possibility of asking various reputable companies to give estimates as to what the cost will be; by a comparison of those estimates we can arrive finally at a conclusion as to what the cost will in fact be as a basic ceiling.
Is not that a wise thing to do?

My hon. friend was not here when the promises were made through the years for the building of this dam. This is a course that can have only one result, to tide over the government during the coming months by advertising for tenders as though it were intended to go ahead. The Prime Minister made it clear this morning that as yet the government had not determined what its ceiling on expenditure would be. He said that it would be impossible to make that determination until he was in position to know what the maximum expenditure would be.
If there was any intention to go ahead it could have been stated in the clearest possible terms that the government was not prepared to go beyond $100 million, or $75 million, or whatever the amount might be. But there is no such promise whatever. The use of the expression "open-ended proposal" applies to the situation here. All we have is an indication that what the government has in mind is to ask various responsible contractors to make an estimate.
But before they can do that they will have to have plans and drawings which would be a lengthy proposition. Then having submitted those plans- to the contractors, it would take months before they could make an estimate. During that interval no doubt there would be a continuation of the investigation that is being made by P.F.R.A. It is passing strange that in his statement the Prime Minister should admit that as yet nothing has been done to ascertain whether or not the figures in the report of the royal commission as to the cost are in line and that the government cannot understand the great divergence between the estimates of the royal commission and those of the P.F.R.A. engineers, and for that reason requires further information.
Personally I think that there should have been a vote provided to cover at least one year's construction. Instead of that, it is apparent that what is going to take place this year will be simply a continuation of what has been taking place in larger or smaller measure from year to year, namely, an expenditure with a view to investigating the potentialities and possibilities of the dam. That is made clear by the letter of the Minister of Agriculture. It is a letter with reference to the interview of almost three years ago. It is dated April 24, 1953 and reads as follows:
Dear Premier Douglas:
My files Indicate that following the receipt of a report from our engineers to the effect that it is possible to construct a dam on the South Saskatche-

wan river at Coteau creek I asked for and had an interview with your government on June 24, 1950.
It was my opinion that because the resources were under the control of the province this information should be made known officially to your government.
We appointed a committee of top officials and engineers associated with the Department of Agriculture to compile the information. Before this report was made public, I again reported to the provincial government on February 2, 1951, indicating that the committee agreed with our engineers that a dam could be built creating a reservoir and that the direct results from such a construction could be irrigation and power generation.
I indicated that the estimated cost of the project would be approximately $101 million on a basis of 1950 costs, divided as follows: $68 million for the dam, $25 million for irrigation and $8 million for power installation. My memory is that you contended that the federal government had left the impression that this was to be a federal undertaking financed by Ottawa. I pointed out that it had been nothing more than a proposal to assist in rehabilitating the drought area and that the only large projects which had been undertaken up to that time, namely, the St. Mary's and Bow River projects, were purely irrigation and the responsibility for financing them was three-way-the federal government stored or made available the water, the province distributed the water over the area and the farmers formed irrigation districts under provincial legislation to distribute the water to the land and administer the districts.
Some question has been raised as to whether or not the provincial government was prepared to accept that. I find it strange-
There is no question in my mind that the provincial government was prepared to accept that.
All right, they are prepared to accept that.
The provincial government, but not this government.

In January of this year a press report appeared in the Regina Leader-Post dealing with what Premier Douglas had said. It is as follows:
Premier T. C. Douglas has reaffirmed the willingness of the province to pay its share of the cost of the South Saskatchewan river project regardless of the unfavourable findings of the royal commission. The premier's statement was contained in a letter to Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent, made in Regina Wednesday.
In the letter he said the province was willing to pay its share of the costs and was preparing a brief setting forth its objections to the findings of the royal commission.
Then the text of the letter is given and it reads in part as follows:
In order that there may be no misunderstanding on anyone's part, may I refer you to my letter to the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner of Feb. 19, 1951, copy of which I am enclosing. At that time the Saskatchewan government expressed its faith in the soundness of the South Saskatchewan river project and declared its willingness to meet its share of the costs.
Supply-Agriculture
We now find ourselves, however, faced with a new proposition in the letter of April 24, 1953, in these words:
-the federal government is prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for co-operation in the project and I am authorized by my colleagues to discuss such a proposal with you once the question of water rights has been settled among the three prairie provinces and agreement reached that the water would be available for the project.
The securing of agreement among the provinces through the water board cannot but postpone action indefinitely.
One day.

Nothing is to be done. The proposal of the provincial government is not to be considered until the water board has made its decision in agreement with the provinces. All these things add up to postponement of action. The Minister of Agriculture said in his letter:
Any proposal put forward by the province should make it clear what contribution to the cost of the dam itself the province is prepared to make to remove any element of federal subsidy for the production of power since power development could obviously not be subsidized in one province unless the federal authorities were prepared to provide similar subsidies in all provinces . . .
The Prime Minister certainly clarified the atmosphere today. Regardless of what the province may say, nowhere is there any undertaking by the federal government as to what liability it is prepared to accept. Nowhere is there a scintilla of evidence or a suggestion by the Prime Minister that the federal government would go ahead, because when asked a very simple question as to the number of dollars of expenditure to which the federal government would limit its responsibility the Prime Minister said: Of course, we cannot assume to state any such figure. In other words, the whole proposition is up in the air today as never before. The concluding words of the Minister of Agriculture in his letter are also very significant. He said:
Any proposal would, of course, have to include some satisfactory means of determining in advance what the total cost of the project would be, and what the federal share of the cost would be.
What does that mean? "Any proposal" refers to any proposal made by the provincial government. Does that mean that the provincial government has to determine what the cost will be? I point out that the letter says:
Any proposal would, of course, have to include some satisfactory means of determining in advance what the total cost of the project would be . . .
Today the Prime Minister says, not by way of conclusive finality but certainly by way of prescient suggestion, that it might be a good

Supply-Agriculture
thing to get in touch with contractors and have them determine the top and bottom levels. In this regard the letter says:
This would be essential so that there was no open-ended commitment which might result in the final costs being far greater than anything either government would regard as reasonable.
That is not necessarily so. There is another simple way. The dominion government could say to the provincial government: We will go ahead with this but we will limit our expenditure to so much money, and if more than that is spent the province of Saskatchewan will be responsible for the excess. That is the only way, and that is why I asked the Prime Minister the simple question today: What is the maximum amount of liability that the dominion government will accept? It could be determined very quickly by the dominion government saying to the province of Saskatchewan: We are prepared to go ahead but if we go ahead and the development requires an expenditure on the part of the dominion government of more than $100 million or $68 million or whatever the figure may ibe, then you will understand that it is your responsibility to cover any excess.
But instead of that we have this open-ended commitment, a beautiful description of the situation. No matter what the province maiy do, the other end is still open for the government to say that it is not responsible in any way for proceeding with the project. Such a system is not satisfactory. It is vague and uncertain. It provides for no promise of completion of the project in any way in the assignable future, or even of the commencement.
I brought this matter up in February and endeavoured to discuss it under irrigation but without success. It was brought up then by way of an 'amendment -and was discussed fully at the time. Some papers did not agree with my stand. I have no Objection to that. One of them was the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, which said:	Give the government a chance
because after aill the session has just nicely started, and with the promises that have been made we have no fear as to the intention of the government to go ahead. They said that, in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister throughout the years has certainly gone no farther than to tell the people of Saskatoon on one occasion about the great potentialities inherent in the proposal to build this dam and1, on the other occasion, of the danger that Saskatoon might be drowned out in the event that the dam did not hold.

On April 1, 1952, the Prime Minister spoke in Regina and there is this report by the Canadian Press:
Prime Minister St. Laurent has been told that the engineering phases of the South Saskatchewan river dam involve "a number of very disturbing features and obvious risks."
Opposition Leader Walter Tucker Tuesday quoted this passage in the Saskatchewan legislature during discussion of a resolution urging quick construction of the dam and irrigation project.
I may be wrong-because the Prime Minister was not in Regina at that time. This was a quotation by Mr. Tucker to the provincial legislature of a statement which the Prime Minister had made. You will notice that Mr. Tucker was pressing for construction and completion of the project. The passage was from a letter written by Mr. G. A. Gaherty to Mr. St. Laurent. Mr. St. Laurent spoke on the extreme high cost of the project and the question of whether the benefits could be more quickly realized in other ways and at less cost to the country. The report continues:
It would seem that the need for utilizing the water of the South Saskatchewan river will increase steadily in the years to come.
Then Mr. Tucker placed responsibility for delay on the provincial government by reason of the fact that there had been a report given by Cass-Beggs. Today the Prime Minister went further along that line than he has ever gone before. He said that after all only one and one-half per cent of the arable land of Saskatchewan would be affected by this project. The quotation of that small percentage indicated a very strong doubt in the mind of the Prime Minister, an almost irrefutable doubt, that the expenditure of the moneys that would have to be expended in this connection would be justified as a national undertaking.
That figure does not tell the picture, Mr. Chairman. One and one-half per cent may be the proper percentage of the province, but there is an area in central Saskatchewan representing five, six or seven thousand acres that will be completely changed. It will blossom as it has never done before except in years when there was rainfall. In addition there will be the start of industrialization of the province through the power development which will be necessary in order to distribute the water-and that will mean a new day for our province.
I said a moment ago that some papers disagreed with me for bringing this matter before the house in February. They said that we should give the government a chance, that it was early in the session. One of those papers was the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. That paper ran an editorial on April 29, the first

editorial on the subject of the exchange of letters between the Minister of Agriculture and the premier of Saskatchewan. The editorial is most revealing.
Mr. Gardiner's suggestion for a new deal on the South Saskatchewan river dam cannot be taken seriously. He has been making speeches about the dam throughout the country ever since 1946. It is altogether too late now for him to discover that Saskatchewan ought to be paying part of the cost of the dam so "that there shall be no element of federal subsidy for the production of power." The production of power was an integral part of the scheme all along. And it was agreed in letters exchanged between Mr. Gardiner and Mr. Douglas that the province should be responsible for the works connected with the power development. Further, it was agreed on the basis of estimates supplied by Mr. Gardiner's own department how these costs should be shared in general terms. Moreover, the terms were suggested by Mr. Gardiner himself and accepted by the province. This, we thought, was settled. Even the royal commission which otherwise showed itself unfriendly toward the project, did not seriously raise the issue of federal participation in the power development. For Mr. Gardiner to raise this and some of the other questions he put in his letter to Mr. Douglas is too obviously a political dodge to cut any ice with the people of Saskatchewan.
May I point out, sir, that is an editorial in a paper which almost consistently supports this government.
Saskatchewan does not expect any preferential treatment in the matter of power. But we do expect at least as good terms as the federal government will offer any other province.
A little later there appears this:
The South Saskatchewan project is primarily a water conservation development to provide irrigation for a dry area in central Saskatchewan. The prime purpose of the dam is to make this water, which is now going to waste, available for irrigation. The irrigation scheme must have first call on the water thus stored and power must be a secondary consideration. Moreover, a substantial block of the power produced at the site will be used by the irrigation scheme itself to pump water to land not reached by gravity. By what yardstick is Mr. Gardiner and the federal government to measure the acceptability of a provincial offer to participate in financing the whole scheme?
That editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix the day before yesterday is the epitome of the attitude taken by both the Leader of the Opposition and myself-and by members of the opposition party to the left in the last few days. It represents the attitude of the people of the province of Saskatchewan without regard to party consideration. The editorial proceeds:
Mr. Gardiner lays down as another condition which the province must meet the stipulation that the provincial proposal must include some satisfactory means of "determining in advance what the total cost would be and . . . the federal share." At first glance, this appears to put on the province the responsibility for doing much of the engineering work leading to the preparation of detailed estimates. But his later remarks about the undesirability of entering an "open-end" agreement
Supply-Agriculture
with the province suggests a basic change in the federal government's policy.
Those are not the views of a partisan; they are the considered views of a paper that, in season and out of season, supports this government-and above everything else supports the need of this dam, so necessary in Saskatchewan. It does on to say:
It has been the government's policy, as in the case of the St. Mary's dam, to rely upon its own engineers' estimates of cost and to assume itself the risk that they may be too low. If Mr. Gardiner is now suggesting that conservation and water development work is to proceed on the basis of a fixed federal contribution, we think a good deal of the necessary work in Canada will be left untouched. The provinces cannot assume these risks half as well as the federal government.
Finally, as I am not excerpting anything, I will read the next paragraph although it does not cover the point of my argument:
Mr. Gardiner has also asked for an outline of the way in which the province proposes to develop the irrigation district once the main dam is complete. This, we have suggested on several occasions, is a reasonable demand upon the province. We urged the province to lay these plans before the royal commission at its Saskatchewan sitting last fall. But the province has not gone beyond the general statement that it is prepared to finance the irrigation works and help the farmers get their land ready. This is not good enough by any means. The province should make its plans now for the full development of the project and announce the stages by which its part would be carried out. We have thought all along this was an essential preliminary to getting federal assistance and we still think so. The provincial government should not hesitate to draft and announce these plans. Its own people are as anxious to know what is involved as the federal government is.
That is the reason I suggested a moment ago that, instead of all this tinkering, all the postponing and monkeying with the project, all the Prime Minister would have to do, if the people of Saskatchewan are to accept it as a fact that the government is going ahead, would be simply to say, We are going to restrict our liability to a certain number of millions of dollars. If the project is proceeded with and the province is prepared to proceed with irrigation and power development, and the cost goes beyond the amount set, that must be assumed by the province.
This editorial continues:
Mr. Gardiner cannot escape announcing a federal policy for the South Saskatchewan river by raising additional questions.
That is the fundamental point I endeavoured to make the other day. When one reads the history of what has taken place, and the discussions during the period I have been in the house, one sees that it has been marked by a series of roadblocks erected on every occasion when the previous one, which was believed to be the last, had been successfully removed. This is another roadblock. The

Supply-Agriculture
Star-Phoenix calls it the raising of additional questions. Then, the final paragraph of the editorial reads:
The reception which the people of Saskatchewan gave to the report of the royal commission should have been enough to tip him off-
That refers to the Minister of Agriculture. -that the people of this province are in earnest about getting some irrigation development started long enough before the next drought to do some good. Moreover the Saskatchewan River Development Association is not leading a delegation to Ottawa this week to be confronted with a new set of conundrums designed to get Mr. Gardiner or the federal government off the hook. We want to know what the federal government proposes to do about the Outlook dam. And we are not inclined to accept more questions as a substitute for action.
Mr. Chairman, that editorial summarizes in full detail the attitude of the people of Saskatchewan. We have waited, as we have had to meet successive roadblocks, and we have removed them. At one time responsibility for irrigation generally and the responsibility for the project was accepted by the dominion government. Later on a question arose as to the responsibility of the province with respect to irrigation, and that was accepted. Then, the question of power came up and it was stated the province should accept the responsibility. Again, that responsibility was accepted. Now, we find that we are back where we started. We have had the P.F.R.A.; we have had a royal commission; we have had water boards; we have had investigations continuing from year to year; and now we are back to the letter of April 24, 1953, which seems to directly suggest, for that is the only interpretation which can be placed upon it, that the provincial government should submit a proposal now in regard to costs.
The letter states:
Any proposal would, of course, have to Include some satisfactory means of determining in advance what the total cost of the project would be, and what the federal share of the cost would be.
Mr. Chairman, it is disillusioning to find that after these years of expectation the people of Saskatchewan are to be met with another postponement, with another alibi, with another proposition which, as the Star-Phoenix says, is new and is unjustified. These words of the Star-Phoenix represent the attitude, as I see it, of the people of Saskatchewan-disappointed, disillusioned and denied that to which they are entitled. The editorial says:
Mr. Gardiner-
I am not casting the blame on him, but he is mentioned as representing the government.
-cannot escape announcing a federal policy for the South Saskatchewan river by raising additional questions.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
We do not want action postponed by a new set of conundrums designed to get the government of Canada off the hook.

Mr. Chairman, it is almost one o'clock so I am not going to make a speech. I simply want to say that there is nothing new in what the hon. member has said. There was nothing new in what the Prime Minister said this morning. He simply repeated what was in the letter and what was in the announced policy of the government in the statement I made last Monday night. I am not going to attempt to review it again to answer the hon. member. I am going to say this, that if anyone will go back and read the whole of the debate to which the hon. member for Lake Centre referred, it will be found that we were discussing exactly the question which he says was never raised before.
The announcement the Prime Minister made this morning was that there was not going to be any construction this year.

He did not say that. He said what any sensible person would conclude, that in a country like ours out in Saskatchewan you probably could not get a crew moving on a job, no matter how you tried to do so, starting at this time. He did not say that there would be no contracts let or nothing done that would indicate the job was going ahead.
That is exactly what he did say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. As it is one o'clock I leave the chair.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

I have a few remarks to make before this item passes. I agree with what has been said this morning as to the great disappointment that will be felt by all people in Saskatchewan over the statement of the Prime Minister, particularly that part in which he said that no matter what steps may be taken this year, in any event construction will not begin.
We know from past experience that we are likely to get more in the way of progressive legislation in the year before an election than for the next three years after an election.
That is the way they do it in Saskatchewan.

I am not saying that is or is not the way they do it in Saskatchewan, but we know from experience that that is the

way it is done here. But apparently on the South Saskatchewan project the expenditure is being done in that way, and we are going to get nothing in the way of construction even this year.
I asked last night how the minister could expect to build the project, or commence to build it, with items in the estimates as small as $636,000. I see from looking over the estimates that I exaggerated the amount that is there that could be used on the South Saskatchewan river development project, because the amount is only $500,000. The Minister of Finance then said that the total item amounted to $7,893,000. But that total item for major irrigation projects is divided as follows:	Bow River irrigation project,
$4,297,000; St. Mary irrigation project, $1,640,000; South Saskatchewan river development, $500,000; Buffalo Pound lake reservoir, $360,000; engineering services for major irrigation and conservation projects, $1,096,000; total, $7,893,000. That is why I asked the Prime Minister this morning what steps the government could take to obtain additional money for construction, because the $500,000 in the estimates certainly was not a sum of money that could be used in any way for construction. To that question the Prime Minister replied that he did not envisage a situation where actual construction could be commenced this year. A little later he said that the best thing that could happen under the so-called proposals he made to Saskatchewan is that final tenders might be called for, and the item in the estimates was for that purpose.
After turning down one possible arrangement, the other would be to make some provision whereby serious tenderers could be invited to make their best bids, with the prospect that they would not be doing so at a loss if their bid were found to be of such an amount that the project could not be proceeded with now. In other words, the proposal to the Saskatchewan government is first of all to ask that government to take steps to prevent an open-ended expenditure by the federal government.
You are asking the provincial government of Saskatchewan for the first time since this project was started to pay part of the construction of the dam and now the Prime Minister says: if we get some kind of an arrangement with the Saskatchewan government we will call for tenders; we will look at the tenders that are submitted and if they are too high we shall have a little money to pay them for the expenses they have incurred' in submitting tenders. In other words, this is a proposal to Saskatchewan, and if Saskatchewan accepts what is apparently implied in 68108-295i
Supply-Agriculture
the proposal, and the terrible financial burden of a huge proportion of the expenditures involved, even then there is no guarantee that construction will begin. All that the province has held out to it is the possibility that tenders will be called for, and if the amount of those tenders is too high, then the Prime Minister will have some money to pay the people submitting the tenders to cover expenses that they have incurred,
I do admire the Prime Minister for making the statement in the way that he did, because he certainly made it in such a manner that it cannot be misunderstood. I do not expect we shall have the government going out to Saskatchewan holding out the possibility that construction may begin this year because, according to the Prime Minister, construction is out of the question.
The Saskatchewan government has been prepared-and I believe still is-to accept its fair share of the cost. It is willing to undertake all the expenditures necessary for the distribution of the water; it is willing to undertake all the expenditures necessary for levelling the land; it is willing to undertake all expenses necessary for the installation of hydroelectric equipment. Even after Saskatchewan has taken this position and has agreed to undertake this large responsibility in order that the project might be commenced and completed, the federal government is now attempting to unload a further large share of the cost without even a guarantee that if the Saskatchewan government accepts the much larger expenses the federal government will go ahead with the project.
I should like to see this government make a concrete proposal to the province of Saskatchewan. A proposal that is concrete sets out the amount of construction that the federal government is prepared to undertake and the amount of 'costs that the federal government is prepared to bear. All this last proposal to the Saskatchewan government is in my opinion is a way of postponing the issue until after the election is held. There is no commitment in it that the dam will be built. The government is reneging on previous understandings, and is now unloading on the province part of the cost of construction of the dam. And even if Saskatchewan would agree to bear a much larger proportion of the cost, there is still no undertaking by the federal government that it will make definite expenditures on this project.
I was disappointed this morning to hear the Prime Minister say, in effect, "Well, after all, according to my estimate this would irrigate only two-fifths of one per cent of the land in Saskatchewan." He seemed to infer

Supply-Agriculture
from that that the project was not of such great importance, after all.
And just on that point I should like to quote Dr. John A. Widtsoe, irrigation commissioner on the royal commission which inquired into the project. He had this to say about the value of irrigation, as set out in an article appearing in The Improvement Era for February of 1953:
The dream of making Saskatchewan a great grain-producing province, growing grain by dry farming, is not a sound dream. It is not sound scientifically; it is not sound economically. A great commonwealth cannot be built on dry farming. You might also write that down in your books-it cannot be done. For Saskatchewan to grow to its destined proportions-I use the word destined deliberately-it must use the water that flows through it to fertilize the soil. That can be done. You have more water in one stream in Saskatchewan than we have in all the streams in my state of Utah if brought together in one stream. Yet we have been able to build a state, and a great state, out of that water.
I say that even if the Prime Minister's figures are correct, and the project would irrigate only two-fifths of one per cent of the land in Saskatchewan, nevertheless according to Dr. Widtsoe it would have the result of building a great province out of the water used in that project.
I feel that at this stage of the session, in the light of the announcement made by the Prime Minister, little can be gained by delaying the passage of this estimate. However, I did wish to rise at this time to say that the people of Saskatchewan will be extremely disappointed. That disappointment was indicated by the editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix placed on Hansard this morning. Irrespective of their political beliefs, the people of Saskatchewan want this project; and I believe if the Minister of Finance would bring in a further supplementary estimate making provision for the beginning of construction this year, he would be making a move which would show the government's proposal really means that the dam is going to be built. And I suggest further that if such a supplementary estimate were brought down it would pass unanimously.
I do not think hon. members are opposed to the project. I think any reservation with respect to it is held by only a few members in the cabinet. In my view that reservation cannot be justified. I do not think the amount of money involved is the deciding factor, because we are all supporting the St. Lawrence seaway development. We understand there has been some difficulty in making a proper agreement with the United States and, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of this morning, the Minister of Transport has stated that if the United States government

does not care to join in a project, then the federal government of this country is willing to undertake not only a project of its own, but a project lying right alongside that of the United States seaway.
So it is not a question of money when it comes to the St. Lawrence seaway. The government is prepared to advance $300 million for that purpose-despite the fact that another deep seaway might be built right alongside the Canadian project. I wish the government would apply that same line of reasoning in connection with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river project. We believe it is a good one; we believe that, for the people of western Canada, it has the same importance as the St. Lawrence seaway to the people of eastern Canada.
The government should not allow the report of a royal commission to stand in its way. The Saskatchewan government is prepared, and for some time has been prepared, to undertake its share of the cost. I would like to see the government of Canada, even at this late stage in the session, bring forward an item sufficiently large to cover any construction which might be undertaken this year. And I believe such an item, accompanied by an agreement, would pass the House of Commons unanimously;

Mr. Chairman,
coming as I do from British Columbia, I am familiar with the development of hydroelectric power on a very wide scale under varying circumstances. In a mountainous region we have tumbling rivers and mighty waterfalls on every hand. We have great water storages already established by nature. I therefore realize the very great problem which confronts the people of Saskatchewan, living as they do in a great tableland, in harnessing such water powers as may be available on the South Saskatchewan river.
We Canadians who live outside Saskatchewan expect to pay part of the cost of this power development and, therefore, we are deeply concerned in the progress of this project. It has taken some years to establish certain engineering data and it will take some further time before it can be reasonably expected to launch this great public work. Some of the speeches I have heard in the house come from hon. members who are most impatient, and who insist that the people of Canada give them a blank cheque at once to go on with this work. In my own province we have learned to be patient in the planning and building of great dams and great hydroelectric projects.
In the Bridge river country we opened recently a new hydroelectric project which

provides the city of Vancouver with most of its power and light. The transmission line in this instance is 120 miles long. Here the water falls some 1,200 feet in a distance of three miles, or about three times higher than Niagara. It took exactly forty years before this project became a reality, from the time the first move was made towards its development. I personally knew Captain Jeffrey Downton, the surveyor who first established its possibilities. Do we expect the government of Canada to move any faster than private capitalists upon such a project?
I was present at the opening of the famous Boulder dam on the Colorado river. It was completed by the United States government after many years of study on the part of that government, and the four states of Nevada, Arizona, California and New Mexico which were concerned in water rights on the Colorado river.
We have the great hydroelectric project in the province of Ontario, which was brought into being following long years of study, research and organization.
In any major operation of this kind, any place in America, it is very unusual for any government or any private group of bankers or industrialists to proceed without the fullest exploration of all phases of the undertaking.
I may say that I support wholeheartedly the proposal to develop the South Saskatchewan river, but I am certainly more interested in a project of equal magnitude which would provide railway service to some thousands of settlers in the Peace river country, who are now handicapped for lack of that service. This is not the time or place to launch a plea for modern rail service for the whole Peace river country including a direct outlet to Pacific ports, but that project has been put before the Prime Minister and the cabinet with some vigour. It is time to say to the people of Saskatchewan not to be weary in well-doing and not to expect the Prime Minister of Canada to issue a blank cheque tomorrow afternoon for the Saskatchewan dam or any other undertaking which has been so loudly supported as a short cut to everlasting prosperity for those immediately concerned.

Mr. Chairman, to listen to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat would make one believe that this is a new project which had just been thought of in the last four or five years. Surveys with regard to this project have been going on for a great many years. It is not a new project at all, it is something on which the dominon government has already spent $3 million in surveys and the obtaining of estimates. I
Supply-Agriculture
do not intend to pursue that angle of the matter any further. I was greatly disappointed in two statements made this morning by the Prime Minister and I am certain the people of Saskatchewan will be equally disappointed. He indicated that this was rather a small matter as far as Saskatchewan was concerned because only two-fifths of one per cent of the agricultural land in the province was involved. That is an indication that the government does not believe that this project is important as far as the economy of Saskatchewan is concerned. That is not correct; it is an important project as far as Saskatchewan is concerned.
We have had drought in that province and it has cost the provincial and dominion governments millions of dollars to ship feed into the province. This was necessary because of the conditions created by the drought. This project would solve that problem at least in part in providing extra reserves of feed in case of drought. We have not had a drought for the last few years, but it will occur again. It has occurred in the past and will recur. This is an important project as far as the economy of Saskatchewan is concerned.
I was also disappointed in the statement by the Prime Minister in which he indicated that apparently he wants Saskatchewan to take the risk that may be involved in any increase in cost over a fixed amount which the dominion government will be prepared to pay. We know that in the last ten years construction costs in Canada have doubled. That was not due to any action by the government of Saskatchewan, it was due to dominion government policy. This government removed controls and at the present time they are increasing interest rates. Those increased costs are the result of policies followed by the federal government.
Is it fair to ask the province of Saskatchewan to assume the risk of any additional cost. It is admitted that this project will take ten years to complete; but how can we know what the costs will be during the last five years of construction? The dominion government controls these costs and they should take the risk of any increase. Those are the two points which I wished to make with respect to this particular matter.
There is another matter about which I should like to get some information from the minister. I indicated last night that I intended to ask some questions with regard to the Pasquia project in northwestern Manitoba being developed under P.F.R.A. I would like to know the cost of this project and the amount spent last year. Will the project be completed this year? What is the agreement with the government of Manitoba with

Supply-Agriculture
respect to the division of costs? What is the agreement between the government of Manitoba and P.F.R.A. with regard to the settling of settlers on this new development?
The question asked by the hon. member for Melfort concerns his section of the province of Saskatchewan.
I was not talking about Saskatchewan. I was talking about the Manitoba section, which is already under construction.

I am quite certain that when the hon. member knows what has happened in Manitoba he will expect exactly the same thing to be done in Saskatchewan. That is why I say it concerns his section of Saskatchewan. The proposal in Manitoba is that we do some diking of the Saskatchewan river to keep water off lands which are being settled. The Manitoba government will be selling this land to settlers who will be brought in.
The Manitoba government have agreed to take some settlers that we will assign from lands that are being evacuated in parts of the drought area. There is no definite undertaking that they will take them all, but they will take some. They have also undertaken to place some returned soldiers. There are quite a number of people already settled on the Manitoba section of the delta.
Under the agreement the greater part of the cost will be paid back to the Manitoba .government through the sale of land. Land is actually sold to these farmers and the agreement stipulates the maximum and minimum prices. The farmers are to pay back a considerable part of the money, and then the greater part of what the federal government pays out is to be returned by the province.
The work will be done by contractors, but the tenders will be called for and the work laid out by P.F.R.A. engineers. We will have charge of the carrying through of the project, but the placing of settlers will be under the Manitoba government as well as the collection of money from the settlers. That government now has the set-up to do that under their settlement plan.
Has the minister a copy of the agreement which he could table?
I have not it here with me and I must say that I am speaking largely from memory. I can have it tabled before the afternoon is out.
I should like to see a copy tabled. Are the settlers now on this land to pay anything extra as a result of the diking being done, or will they receive this benefit free of cost?

The people who are on the land have an agreement with the Manitoba

government. The Manitoba government sold them the land and they will have to pay the amounts which have been arranged for between them and the government under the deals they have made. I am not in a position at the moment to give the exact details, but I think they will all be covered in the agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this item because reference was made to a statement which I had made in 1949 and I should like to clarify it. It will be remembered that on October 13, 1949, as reported on page 761 of Hansard, I outlined the plight in which cities like Regina and Moose Jaw found themselves on account of a water shortage. I gave some of the historical background and indicated that when the agreement was made with the Canadian Pacific to build through western Canada they had agreed to follow the line of fresh water. But they were diverted from their original intentions and built their line through the southern part of Saskatchewan, leaving water at Brandon and going straight to Medicine Hat before they came to water again. As a consequence of that breach of contract cities and other places like Regina, Moose Jaw, Swift Current, Gull Lake and Maple Creek which were in between found themselves actually short of water. I tried to impress on parliament when I spoke that the federal government had some responsibility to the people who had settled there because the railways had been allowed to depart from the original contract.
At that time I was having a discussion in Regina with the city, provincial and federal governments with respect to the responsibility for extending assistance to the city in building its water supply system. I had difficulty at first. The provincial government stated that it was the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government pointed out that it was a municipal responsibility, that when a municipality was unable to carry out its own responsibilities it should appeal to the provincial government, and if the provincial government was unable to complete the project it could call upon the federal government. After several attempts I finally succeeded in bringing the three governments together. I think we had two conferences. Nothing came of the first one. All parties stood pat, refusing to accept any responsibility.
After further discussions I succeeded in getting the federal government to promise that it would keep water in Buffalo Pound lake in the Qu'Appelle valley in perpetuity for Regina and Moose Jaw. What that involved remains to be seen. If we build the Saskatchewan river dam in the years to

come, the water will flow there naturally. If it is not built, the federal government has the responsibility of building pumping stations on the Saskatchewan river and keeping a level of water in Buffalo Pound lake and the Saskatchewan valley sufficient to supply the needs of Regina and Moose Jaw, and also stock watering and irrigation projects farther down the Qu'Appelle valley. This will be an expensive undertaking.
I am pleased to say that as a result of that undertaking the city of Regina has gone ahead with the work. There is a dam at Buffalo Pound lake where a considerable body of water is impounded. A power station and a pumping station have been built in the valley to pump water up to the refining beds and works about five miles inland from Buffalo Pound lake. From there Moose Jaw will build a pipe line and obtain its water supply. At the present time we are trying to build a 36-inch pipe line from the site of the filtration beds to Regina city, a distance of thirty-six miles. Hon. members may have noticed that on account of steel being in short supply- I do not want to cast any reflection on the company-it was decided to build the line with another type of pipe, and this has led to great disappointments. At present the project is delayed slightly on that account.
But the most important thing is that within the next year we will have an adequate water supply in Regina. I had indicated that it was the responsibility of the government to assist us with this project because through the oversight of earlier governments the C.P.R. had been allowed to build so far south. At that time I also emphasized the importance of irrigation to the central dry part of Saskatchewan. I do not blame the Prime Minister for saying that just 250,000 acres will be affected. He cannot be an authority on everything. But we who live in western Canada know that the creation of a reservoir in the centre of Saskatchewan of the size and nature that is contemplated and the irrigation of half a million acres of land will improve the agricultural and grazing possibilities of many millions of acres of land. It will permit the production of fodder on which we can winter our stock, and the stock can spend the spring and summer on dry pastures. It will change the nature of agriculture in that part of the country.
I hear many people talk about a great industrial development in that part of the country. Personally I cannot see it. To have industrial development you must have markets. We have a small population. I am not sure what industries can be established there that will thrive. Certainly any of the industries that the C.C.F. government has tried to bring to Saskatchewan to date
Supp ly-A griculture
have proved to be dismal failures. The last one, the woollen mills in Moose Jaw, failed the other day. I do not want this to be a political discussion. Coming from Saskatchewan, I certainly am pressing for the federal government to assume a great part of the cost. I know what the people there have gone through in past years. The wealth of Saskatchewan, compared with that of other parts of the country, is very small. In fact it seems to me that we create wealth to build big insurance offices, banks and so on in eastern Canada. Be that as it may, I think I should clarify something at this point. At that time I was pressing, as were other members, to have the federal government assume as much responsibility as I could get it to take. After the debate had gone on for some time, the Minister of Agriculture had this to say, as found at page 770 of Hansard for October 13, 1949:
What we say in regard to that is this, that the provincial government ought to share some of the capital cost, which reduces the total cost per acre from some $40 or $50 down to the $10 that the farmer can pay, and that no part of that money ought to be collected back from the farmer. We say the federal government should put up something and the provincial government should put up something: and whatever that amount is, it should be charged up to the capital cost which the farmer is not going to be required to pay, in order that his costs may be reduced down to the $10.
My personal opinion about that is that when you take all the works for which we are responsible, including the original dam, we would be assuming far more than our total responsibility, whatever that responsibility might be based upon, whether it is a legal responsibility or a national responsibility. We would not be very far from the mark if the provincial government became responsible for half of the cost and the federal government became responsible for the other half.
Does the minister suggest that for the South Saskatchewan project, also?

I have told my hon. friend that whatever we finally decide with the Alberta government as being the principle to be applied will be applied to all of them.
I think the Minister of Agriculture made his position quite clear then. I do not say it filled me with enthusiasm because I wanted to get more for Saskatchewan. I was quoted this morning as having said that I was under the impression that the federal government was going to build the dam and that the distribution of water was going to be the responsibility of the provincial government. I do not think I made any reference to where the responsibility for power should lie. I only wish to say one other thing. I am as anxious to see the dam constructed as anyone is. I know its national value. I know that the economic value of such a project will be enjoyed not only by the people of Saskatchewan but by the people of Canada as a whole.

Supply-Agriculture
I doubt if we have the finances in Saskatchewan at present to permit us to go ahead and complete the entire project, but I am not going to be unduly critical. I can see the point of view of the Prime Minister and people in eastern Canada when they say, especially in view of the royal commission report, that the project has to be closely studied. I can see that they do not wish to embark on some project that involves producing power free for one province when they may be called upon to do the same for others. Therefore I can see why they hesitate. These people are sincere in their desire to obtain the best deal they can get on such a project, and when we find the government sympathetic towards it, when we find all members of the house, including those from Quebec and Ontario, sincerely sympathetic towards the project, I do not think we will help it very much if we try to make it a political football.

Mr. Chairman, I said before lunch that I did! not want to make any more speeches on this project during this session if I could help it. However, I would just like to suggest to members of the committee, no matter what part of Canada they icome from, that they should get a copy of the report on prairie farm rehabilitation and related activities for 1951-1952. It is the last annual report, it has been tabled in the house, and it is available to everyone. When you have it I would ask you to turn to page 14 and, on the page opposite, you will find a map of the three western provinces. On that map there is drawn what is known as the Palliser triangle or the P.F.R.A. area. One of the things that have caused people to want to take another look at the matter after having read the report of the commission is that the report says there ought to be a survey made of that area. The map shows a dot for every one of the small water projects which are already there, and there are 38,000 of them shown. Forty-eight thousand are now completed but there were 38,000 up to the time of this report. Those water projects are spotted on the map, which is so completely covered that there is hardly any more room for dots. You must remember that we have lined up for a time ahead 1,500 more projects per year, in order to fill in some of the areas where there are no dots.
My argument in connection with that phase is that we have had a pretty complete survey of that area. Our engineers have walked over every farm and have made a survey. I think it is a stronger position for those of us who come from western Canada to say that somebody, it does not matter whether it is
[Mr. McCusker.l
an incoming government, an outgoing government, the present government or any government, should do this job. The surveys are pretty well completed and everything we need in the way of information is there, and I suggest that a study of the map I have referred to will convince a lot of people. There is another document which I think that every member should get-and I was sorry that more did not get it. When we came to the end of giving relief because of the drought, as head of the department I took the responsibility of recommending to the government that we hire a man to write a report. We employed a man who is known to everyone in western Canada-Dr. Stapieford. He had been the principal of Regina College and he had been associated with some of the work. He wrote a report and I have piles of copies down in the department and I wish that members would come and get them; because after reading that report they would know a lot more about this project than they do now.
When people have said to me that the report of the commission indicates that this whole project is just on the fringe of drought, that this lake that we are proposing to put in is just on the fringe of relief, I have asked them to turn to pages 28, 29, 30, 31 and so on of the report which show maps of the areas where we had to pay relief.
Too bad the Prime Minister has not seen it.
The Prime Minister has seen it and he has gone over it carefully. That is one of the reasons why he said what he did say to you this morning.
Oh, I see.

If hon. members can see this map from where they sit they will notice that the dam is right in the middle of the dark area-the proposed dam; it is not there yet. The lake that would be put there would be right in the middle of the area. The report says that it is on the fringe, and I can understand people coming to a certain conclusion when the facts are not known about it. I would like every member to get a copy of the report and they will see where relief which cost us $186 million was required. That is more than twice the amount which those of us who know this project think the lake is going to cost. When one takes a look at all of the facts he can more easily be convinced than by simply arguing over what I said or what somebody else said a long time ago. I feel very satisfied with myself because I have had more to do with getting everybody

thinking about the project than has any other one person.
Hear, hear.

I do not suppose that I am going to be around until everyone is benefiting by the project, but as long as I am around I am going to keep right on talking favourably of it and not trying to introduce ideas that will slow up its arrival. Simply accusing me of slowing it up will in fact have that effect, because there has been no one trying to speed it up more than I have. People who go around saying that the Minister of Agriculture is trying to slow the thing down, and who try to convince a lot of people out in western Canada that the Minister of Agriculture would be less likely to support it, are not helping to promote the project. Anyone who says that I am trying to slow it down just does not know anything about my thinking or my activities either-or they are just trying to picture my attitude to help them when running their election. I am not going to say anything more about it and I am going to rely upon the people of Saskatchewan to realize that what the hon. member for Regina City read a moment ago represents the situation as I have stated it all the way through.
One more thing should be said at the moment in view of the discussion this morning. It is all very well to take the Star-Phoenix and read an editorial from it, and my hon. friend was trying to infer from the reading of it that the editorial writer was some friend of the Liberal party or myself. Well, my hon. friend knows that the editor of the Star-Phoenix is not a friend of his party or of our party either. The previous editor of the Star-Phoenix died two or three months ago. The editorials that had been written up to that time were written by a very able and competent editorial writer who had a certain point of view that was described this morning. However, the gentleman who is writing the editorials now is not that man. I am not going to say anything critical of the man who wrote the editorial this week other than to point out that it was not the man who previously wrote the editorials. He is a new man and his point of view will no doubt be answered by some other people; and for the time being that is all I want to say about that matter.

Mr. Chairman, I have refrained from taking any part in this debate because I felt that it would have been over long before this. The remarks made a short time ago by the hon. member for Cariboo have made me believe that I, coming from the east coast, should say a few words.
Supply-Agriculture
I have been here as a member for eight years and in that time there has never been a project of a national character of any kind which has come before this house that I did not support; and I am prepared to support other projects of a national character when I am convinced that they are economically sound.
I believe that the people of this country will be convinced that in the statement which the Prime Minister made this morning he was most frank and honest.
Hear, hear.

Many people might have expected, when the questions were being asked this morning, that the Prime Minister might have risen and tried to play some politics over this project-as has been done since last November. I believe that when people in the country read his remarks they will be convinced that he replied with what he believed to be honest facts that he had before him, and in no way can there be any suggestion about his playing politics.

I would like to ask my hon. friend if he would not add that the conclusion he would draw from hearing the Prime Minister speak on this subject today, or on any occasion when he has spoken of it, is that he has been trying to leave the impression that he is very friendly to it.

I can endorse that statement wholeheartedly. On every occasion upon which I have heard him speak of the project, he has taken that stand, that if the cost of this project was in line with the benefits that may accrue, he was prepared to support it. In his statement this morning he said that we must realize that it is the moneys of the people of Canada that must be provided to take care of the cost of this project. He must be convinced that it is the right thing to do before he can endorse it.
Now, I would be prepared to endorse it when I am convinced that it is the proper thing to do. Statements have been put on the record which would indicate that there have been promises made in other parts of Canada by members of this House of Commons. These promises might be helpful at election time. They are, however, somewhat in the same position as the dog who was reaching for the shadow and lost the bone; they might be more harmful in other parts of Canada. There is little doubt in my mind that there will be quotations from this debate at election time in the maritime provinces. I am quite sure that there will be. In other words, people would indicate, and they would have the facts before them, that we in this House of Commons were ready to go ahead with this project without all the information

Supply-Agriculture
that might be necessary before a start could be made. I believe such a statement was made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that if we were all convinced it was a sound investment we would all endorse it.
The same hon. member suggested a short time ago that a further amount should be provided in the supplementary estimates to get this project under way immediately. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I could not endorse that. I have read the report of the South Saskatchewan commission, and from the information I have been able to obtain from other sources I could not support this project now. In advocating that there should be an amount put in the supplementary estimates now to get this project going just as soon as possible, the hon. member fails to understand the position in which he is placing other members of the House of Commons from other parts of this country.
Before I take my seat, I want to say again that I believe the statement made this morning by the Prime Minister was the statement of an honest and sincere man. The people of this country will weigh that statement very carefully. I am sure they will endorse the stand he has taken and will be prepared to wait until all the necessary information is available before a decision is made. I do believe that when that time comes, if it is decided that we should go ahead with the project, it will have the support of the maritime members, the western members and the members from central Canada.

May I lay on the table the documents that were requested by the member for Melfort? I am suggesting that we put in the order in council as well as the agreement. I cannot place these documents on the table until the Speaker is in the chair, but in any case I shall send them over and the hon. member can look at them and see that they are placed on the table.
What is the nature of the documents?

I want to add this, and I do not do so in any political sense whatever. I have been in political life for 40 years, and I have been working with a lot of people in that time. I want to say to the members of this house and to the people of Canada in general, and the western people in particular, that I have never worked with anyone in whom I would have greater faith, if we presented our case in a suitable manner, than the Prime Minister. I know he would be friendly and helpful to it. I do not want anyone to think that any discussions I have had with him have left any other impression with me than that if we ever had anyone at the head of the government who would be 
friendly to a proposal of that kind, it is the present Prime Minister. If we put our case properly, and if we have as good a case as some people think we have or even as good a case as I think we have, I do not think we need to be making all these pessimistic prophecies concerning what is going to happen to it in the future.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that everything has been said about this dam that possibly could be said. It is for that reason that 1 shall occupy only a moment or two in endorsing what has been said by my colleagues the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Assiniboia. I would say that the new and significant thing that has taken place today has been the statement by the Prime Minister. I agree with one hon. member who has said it was an honest, forthright statement, and as such I welcome it. But it means that we in Saskatchewan now know, as from this morning, that we are to be disappointed in connection with the matter of construction for this year.
I have lived, of course, in the city of Saskatoon for some time. I am not, in the ordinary sense, a rural member although I have a good deal of rural territory in my constituency, which I am told I am to lose in this redistribution. I need not point out to hon. members in this house that any city in western Canada is dependent for its prosperity upon the prosperity of all those rural workers and farmers who are contiguous to it. I believe, therefore, it is very much my business, as the representative of the centre of a great farming community, to say my few words here today in support of what has already been said for the building of this dam.
I was going to say a word about the minister's last statement concerning his 40 years in politics. I was going perhaps to comment upon what history will say about the effect of that intervention of the minister upon the politics of Saskatchewan, but I think I shall leave them for a future occasion. I want to say that I am very disappointed that nothing will be done this year, according to the Prime Minister's statement, and I take it at its face value. With that, sir, I shall leave it for this time.

I do not want to allow this item to pass without paying a compliment to the work of P.F.R.A. in Saskatchewan. I believe that they have done excellent work in that province over the past few years. We may have disagreed about some minor details, but certainly the over-all work done by P.F.R.A. has been of immense benefit to the Palliser triangle and even outside the

Palliser triangle. That this work has been of benefit is indicated by the fact that all parts of western Canada are endeavouring to have the P.F.R.A. extended. I represent an area of the province which has never benefited from P.F.R.A. to any great extent. Over the years I have had numbers of letters from municipalities and individuals asking that their particular area be included in the P.F.R.A. area.
I have in my hand the submission to the government by the farmers' unions of western Canada. In that they state:
We would also urge favourable consideration by this government in extending the benefits of P.F.R.A. to other prairie areas, including the Peace river block.
I think that not only should the P.F.R.A. be extended to the rest of the prairie provinces, but perhaps it should be extended to the whole of Canada. The conservation program that has been carried out by P.F.R.A. in the area in which it has operated is something that could be duplicated-perhaps not in exactly the same manner because it has operated in the drought area-in the rest of Canada. What consideration is the government giving to extending the P.F.R.A. to other areas in the dominion?

Before answering the last question I want to thank the hon. member for the finest eulogy that I have ever had since I have been in public life. I have been administering P.F.R.A. and selecting the staffs now for 17 years, and there is not a single policy that they have followed that I did not either originate or pass upon by putting my signature to the suggestions of my officials. Therefore, I take it that an expression of appreciation of the kind that we have just heard, from the source from which it has come, is one of those things which one appreciates as he goes through public life. I want to express my appreciation of those remarks, more particularly since they will be on Hansard.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And they will be on every telephone pole.

Having said that, I would say to him that P.F.R.A. was set up as a program to rehabilitate the area known as the Palliser triangle, the area that I was indicating on the map a few moments ago. As has been stated, a good job has been done there by my officials, and people outside think that we ought to extend it to other parts of western Canada at least, and some people believe it ought to be extended to all of Canada. Again I would not have any objection to that. Back in 1943 a committee of the house sat on the matter, examined into it and made a recommendation
Supply-Agriculture
that that be done. The main reason why it has not been done up to the present is that it was thought advisable to take all the money that we could obtain for the time being and deal with the problem which we started out to deal with. I am sure that as soon as we can get through dealing with the South Saskatchewan river dam and have it at the stage one way or other where we can say it is going to be done or it is not, and so soon as we add to that the consideration of the Red Deer project, which is another that is very close to the hearts of quite a few members sitting on the other side as well as some sitting on this side of the house, when we have dealt with these- these are the last two large projects that have been passed upon by P.F.R.A. engineers-when we get to that point, I have no doubt that consideration will be given to the question as to whether we are to extend the act into further activities elsewhere; but for the time being it is not the intention of the government to put through legislation extending it.

I hesitate to rise again, but I think the answer given by the Minister of Agriculture is very typical. He takes all the praise to himself that I was giving to the officials who had carried out the program.
You did not know whom you were praising.

I can assure him that I was praising the officials who carried out the conservation program. With respect to the policy of P.F.R.A., I want to say this. I am one who does not believe in not giving credit where credit is due.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Don't take it back.
That is exactly what I was doing; I was giving credit to the officials for the way in which this program was carried out.

I am not going to enter into this competition for credit, although P.F.R.A. was set up by the Bennett government. But as between the minister and the hon. member for Melfort, that question has been determined. I should like to ask the minister one question which has to do with the expenditures under P.F.R.A., in connection with investigational work, and so forth, on the South Saskatchewan project back in 1949, and I want to have the record brought up to date. In 1949 a question was asked in the house as follows, as reported at page 826 of Hansard:
What amount of money was spent prior to March 31, 1948, by P.F.R.A. in connection with investigational work on the South Saskatchewan project?
What amount of money was spent from April 1, 1948, to March 31, 1949, . . .

Supply-Agriculture
What amount has been spent or is actually committed to be spent April 1, 1949, to September 30, 1949 . . .
So that the record will be complete, the answer as to the amount of money spent prior to March 31, 1948, in connection with the work is $296,447.87. The amount spent between April 1, 1948, and March 31, 1949, was $143,212.76; the amount spent between April 1, 1949, and September 30, 1949, was $634,308.25.
What has been spent each year since, including 1949 to date, on this project?

I am sorry I am not able to give it year by year. The total amount spent on the South Saskatchewan river project from 1935 to 1951 is $1,733,318; and from 1951 to 1952 the total is $510,144. The grand total is $2,243,462. But in view of the discussion that took place this morning I should point out that in the Hansard which'-*
The minister did not give the amount for 1952-53.
That is 1951.
What was the expenditure for 1952-53?
The treasury figures are not out yet for that but it is estimated at half a million dollars. The total figures are not out.
That would be from April 1-
The amount set out last year for this particular project was $1 million, but we did not spend $1 million on the project last year. I was going to point out-
Does that mean that in the last year, April 1952 to April 1953, the estimated amount to be spent was $500,000?
The estimate was $1 million.
The minister said it would be around $500,000.

Yes, it would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of half of what was voted last year. When this discussion started first, back in 1949, in the debate that was put on the record this morning we find the following: It starts out as a quotation of the estimate itself, that is the major irrigation and water conservation projects in the prairie provinces consisting of $7,500,000.
What page?

It appears on page 761 of Hansard of October 13, 1949. The item was divided in this way:
St. Mary Irrigation project, $2,900,000.
Bow River irrigation project, conditional upon satisfactory agreements with the province of Alberta

and others, $2 million. South Saskatchewan river irrigation project:
And I would call attention to the description from here on.
Engineering surveys, land use and economic surveys and other investigational work, $2 million.
That is, we were definitely told in that vote that this was purely an investigational work, and that there could not be under that vote anything in the nature of construction work, or even preparation for construction. We were told that definitely, in the way it was drafted.
Then it goes on to make another item for surveys and engineering which had to do with the Red Deer diversion. But it was surveys and engineering, and nothing more. In the item this year the South Saskatchewan, as it was last year, is put in along with the Bow River and the St. Mary dam, in the same wording and under the same classification. And there is construction being carried on under those classifications.
And that is just exactly why it was said by the Minister of Finance last night, by myself and by the Prime Minister again this morning, that he is not saying definitely that nothing is going to be done that may lead up to construction. Neither am I. The wording of the item itself makes that a possibility. But he did say, and quite truthfully-as he is always truthful when he speaks either in the House of Commons or anywhere else- that it is rather difficult to conceive of circumstances, in view of all the facts, under which there could be any construction this year. And everyone has said that during all the time it has been discussed.

There is one other matter in connection with expenditures about which I should like to ask the minister. In a return brought down the other day in connection with expenditures made for what was described as counsel in connection with the South Saskatchewan river project, or counsel of the royal commission, there was an item of $35,000 to the Mannix company: What was the nature of the work done by the Mannix company for the royal commission?

The work done by the Mannix company was the figuring out of the whole cost as it was written into the report. That is, they set it all up. Some suggestion was made by the member for Lake Centre a moment ago that it would be difficult to make a tender, because of certain things not having been done. Mannix and company set down that information now available, and really made out what to all intents and purposes would be a tender.

Mr. Chairman, I would be less than generous if I did not say a word of commendation of the work carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in the constituency I represent. I want to say here and now, in rebuttal of what was said a moment ago by the Iron, member for Mel-fort, that the work in the Dauphin district, where there has been rehabilitated by P.F.R.A. about a quarter of a million acres, was done for less than a million dollars.
If the report is correct, that in connection with the South Saskatchewan project only about a quarter of a million acres could be irrigated within the next twenty years, even with the construction of a dam, I would point out that the work done in the Dauphin district cost about one per cent of what it is reported would be the cost of doing the same kind of work in connection with the Saskatchewan river dam.
I am not condemning the project at all; but it does seem to me that in the light of the 38,000 or more projects which have already been completed under the act, and at a cost much less than the estimated cost of the South Saskatchewan project, the right thing to do would be to proceed with smaller projects, such as the one at Dauphin and at Pasquia Flats in northwestern Manitoba. Projects of that kind would cost only a fraction of the reported cost of the Saskatchewan dam.
I would hope eventually that the dam on the Saskatchewan river would be completed. I must say I was most impressed by the statement made this morning by the Prime Minister. It was logical, fair and friendly, and I could not conceive how any hon. member could criticize it. What more could he say? He did not say it would not be built, nor did he say that it would be built immediately. The hon. member for Assini-boia made the comment-and I was tempted to reply to him-that the Prime Minister had said it would not be built. What he did say was that he would not promise it could be built immediately-at least, that was my understanding of his statement.
May I say a word of commendation of what the Minister of Agriculture did for us. It will be agreed that he has excellent officials in his department, particularly those who are connected with P.F.R.A. I have known and met them, and I have worked with them. They are excellent men; but I wonder who selected them. Who appointed them? Of course it was the Minister of Agriculture.

detail an experience we had in our district. In 1947 we suffered from a disastrous flooding condition. The Dauphin valley runs between two ranges of mountains, each about 100 miles in length. In that year there were heavy rains in June; on one night there was about nine inches of rain in the- mountain area. The result was a serious condition of flooding.
I got in touch with Ottawa, by telephone, and spoke to the Minister of Agriculture, inviting him to come to Dauphin.
