I indicated to the minister on an earlier occasion that I would have something to say concerning prairie farm assistance. In line with the compliments that have been passed around in the last few minutes, I should like to thank the minister for his personal interest in attending to several cases I sent to him. I hope he does not use that little compliment in the election campaign against me, but I am sure he will not run in Macleod anyway. I appreciate the work of any minister who will take an interest in individual cases and try to do the best he can to solve things for you. However, I do not think that ministers can take very much credit for all the technical things that may have to be worked out by their officials.
I remember when I was a boy my father bought me an old plug pony of which I was very proud except that its hoofs were pretty well flattened out and I did not like that at all. I went to a blacksmith shop and asked the blacksmith if I could take some

old horseshoes from the scrap pile outside. He told me to help myself. I picked out four horseshoes which I thought would fit the old plug, borrowed some nails from the blacksmith, and went home and tried to put those old shoes on the horse.
My father came along and asked me what I was doing and I told him that I was trying to fix up the hoofs a little bit. He looked at me and he said, "You will never do anything there; you cannot do it that way." I told him that I thought I could. That afternoon my mother took me out in the country and it was dark when we got back. The next morning I went to the pasture to get my old pony and was greatly surprised to see it had brand new shoes on its hoofs, all polished up. By Jove, I thought, that was fine and lovely. I brought the old plug up and was admiring it when my father came along and said, "By Jove, son, I never thought you could do it." Of course, it was not I who had done it, neither is it the minister who gets on a grader or looks through the spyglass of an instrument. What he does perhaps is just to get on the telephone. But I appreciate the cases that the minister has taken up for me.
I should like to ask two questions. They are quite different but I do not want to have to rise twice in my place. One or two farmers in my constituency have suggested that perhaps the P.F.A.A. might be used to institute some plan of hail insurance for farmers on an individual basis. I am quite cognizant of the fact that this act would operate where an area met the qualifications for assistance. Hail insurance companies do not base their hail insurance on an area; they insure individual farms.
A suggestion was made to me that some farmers might not be adverse to paying another one-half of one per cent on their grain sales to have such a measure. I am not advocating it; I am not saying whether it should or should not be done. But some farmers have approached me and suggested that there might be some plan worked out to insure individual farmers against losses from hail.
I suppose it would have to be the equivalent of a compulsory bail insurance plan, and that is why I say that I do not particularly favour it nor am I against it. All I am saying is that some farmers have come to me and asked if something of the kind could not be worked out. I should like to get the minister's reaction. I should like to ask him if any survey has been made-he has been talking about other types of surveys lately- among the farm population to find out whether they would be agreeable to such a


plan. If there is a general feeling among farmers and farm unions that something like that should be done, then I think the government should give some consideration to at least looking over the situation and getting statistics to see whether or not it would be beneficial to the majority of farmers.
I should like to deal now with another matter which comes under this item which has to do with prairie farm assistance. I have brought one or two cases to the attention of the minister and I believe they are under consideration. I am not going to mention them in particular, but they are farmers who have occupations other than that of farming. Because they have other occupations they have been denied benefits under P.F.A.A., even though their crop yields qualified them for benefits.
I am aware that the cases I brought forward have been dealt with carefully. I have no criticism to make of the consideration that has been given to cases I have brought before the minister or the officials. I do not know of any case that has been dealt with unfairly. I think the officials looked at those cases and attempted to reach as fair a decision as they could within the provisions of the act. I believe they went as far as their responsibilities would1 permit them to go. In fact, on one or two occasions I think they attempted to see if they could not work some farmer into the act. As I say, I am not critical of that at all.
But there are cases where farmers are denied benefits because they are in receipt of some other income which is legitimately earned from an occupation other than farming. Perhaps I might mention one case and I hope it will not prejudice it. I use it only as an illustration. A young school teacher got married and decided to go into farming. He and his wife bought a farm and as they had not the cash to pay for it they assumed a mortgage. They bought machinery for which they went into debt. Of course anyone doing this is always taking a sort of gambling chance on whether he is going to get a crop, what his yield will be, whether he will be hailed out, whether the grasshoppers will come along, whether frost will ruin his crop, and so on.
In the course of time this school teacher reached the point where he could not see how he could pull through and pay all his debts. So he got a job teaching school and taught for a while, but he still ran the farm. He did not have someone else come in to run it. He worked as best he could af ter school hours. He was there Friday night and he worked on Saturday. His wife worked. She drove tractors and did all she possibly could.

What happened? At the end of the crop year they were flooded out and did not get a crop. As a result they came within the act so far as yield was concerned and were entitled to prairie farm assistance. The case is now before the board of referees, or whatever it is called. The reason that assistance was not paid to him as it was to others was that he had some other income. I hope it will be paid to this young man. I only give this case as an illustration. There may be hundreds of similar cases. As a matter of fact I have another case but it does not involve a school teacher.
I do not want to prejudice any case, but I would urge that in deciding all these matters those in authority, whether it be the original officials handling prairie farm assistance or the board of referees, should be very liberal in their interpretation of that part of the act and do all they can to give assistance where assistance is needed, not merely because these people come within the act by reason of yield but also because they may be in very straitened circumstances.
In the case I have mentioned it is easy to suppose that the young gentleman regarded the employment he took as temporary, and that he expects to eventually build up his farm and make a good farm out of it. Perhaps he may acquire a little more acreage, and it may be that his ambition is to be a good farmer. In such cases I think those in authority should give the widest possible interpretation to the act. I should like the minister to express his views on these two points.

On the first point, having to do with hail insurance, the question involved was decided back in 1910 when hail insurance was proposed in western Canada. Representations were made that such insurance should be provided by the federal government. It was determined then, as it would be now, that insurance is a provincial and not a federal matter. Three different commissions were set up, one in each of the prairie provinces, to deal with the question of hail insurance. The whole question of insurance is involved in that one decision. If we had attempted to put on insurance of any kind it would have been declared ultra vires and we could not have carried on with it.
When we started to set up a scheme of prairie farm assistance we had to devise a plan which was not insurance. The only way we could make sure that it was not insurance was to collect the money necessary to carry on the scheme in some other way than charging fees to individuals. Therefore we set up the present system. We did that after having advocated some crop insurance scheme for 50 years without being able to devise anything that would suit or that could be carried on
Supply-Agriculture
by the provinces by way of insurance. The loss that occurred when the whole crop of a province was wiped out was such that the province did not have anything to pay anything with. Therefore, whatever the plan was, it had to cover a much wider area, so the plan was made national in scope and was applied in the way in which it now operates. It could not possibly be insurance because we could not do that under a national plan. We do not want to get involved in trying to establish hail insurance under this plan because it would probably put us in the position where the scheme itself would be declared ultra vires.
As to the other question, we have threshed that out in at least a thousand cases ever since the plan was set up in 1939. In every one of them we have had to come to the conclusion that we would again destroy the plan if we were to say that a person who is running an elevator, for example, who is spending practically his full time running an elevator and has his family on a farm, were to be given what to all intents and purposes is government assistance in order to carry on his farm. We just do not feel that is involved in this plan. Whether it is a school teacher, a man who runs a store, a station agent, as many of these people are who make claims, or an elevator operator who perhaps lives on his farm but goes into town to operate the elevator or only goes over to a railway siding to operate the elevator, we say the fact that he is drawing money in that way puts him in the position of the man in Montreal who helps to pay.
It is all very well to say that he pays into it because he grows a little grain, and that he should have a chance to draw out because he produces grain, but the fellow in Montreal also pays in and does not get the chance to draw anything out. He pays in because it has been adopted as a national scheme to take care of people in very difficult circumstances as the result of a lost crop. It is assumed that the school teacher in the district who is being paid by the very people who have lost crops, or the elevator operator who is being paid out of handling whatever grain there is, is in the same position as these other people throughout the country.

I am not saying that the general idea should be completely done away with and that everyone should get the benefit of the act whether or not he works. I am not suggesting that. I am suggesting that cases perhaps could be judged on the basis of a means test of some kind. I think there is a little difference between a man who may have an interest in a farm but lives in Montreal, draws a yearly salary and never goes to his farm-

There are one or two matters which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It is my understanding that under the P.F.A. Act, where wheat is grown in a district, wheat is used in order to determine the eligibility of a given area. The farmers in the particular section of Alberta which I happen to represent cannot understand that. There is little wheat grown in the area, and farmers feel that the department is not justified under the act in using wheat to determine eligibility. It is substantially a coarse grains area, barley being the principal grain grown. The feeling everywhere in the area is that it is a complete injustice to use wheat to determine eligibility. I have talked to certain inspectors and they have expressed the same view to me. These


inspectors have indicated to me that it is beyond their comprehension why wheat is used in that particular area to determine eligibility. After I have brought another matter forward the minister might like to comment on that problem.
The other matter I have to raise concerns the P.F.A.A. and I realize, as we have been told often enough, that it was not designed as an insurance scheme. I have not recognized it as such. When the act was first brought in the government had in mind crop losses resulting from drought. Later the provisions were extended so that hail could come under the act. In the Red Deer area we have not suffered as a consequence of loss by drought but in 1951, for example, we did lose very heavily as a consequence of hail.
It is the general feeling among farmers there that the regulations with respect to eligibility of an area, and the determination of whether or not a township is covered for drought, do not make too much sense as applied to hail. Generally speaking, drought hits and harms an entire area. With hail it is a case of hop, skip and jump. I have seen some most fantastic patterns. For example, we had 12 sections in the south end of a township which were hailed out 100 per cent. Those in sections 1 to 11 were paid, yet the three farms in the twelfth section were completely excluded from the act. The reason was that the authorities were able to develop some kind of an ineligible block extending from the north which took in that one section.
These farmers feel, as they have said to me during the course of our discussions, that probably the time has arrived when some consideration could be given to a change in the regulations as they apply to hail. I realize and I repeat that this is not an insurance scheme, but these farmers say that if the department were to decrease the area or size of the block under which P.F.A.A. might be paid they would be willing to pay considerably more than the present levy. That would not be a change in the principle of the act. Whether they pay 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent the size of the payment does not change the principle underlying the act, and a degree of fairness might be brought into P.F.A.A. as it applies to hail.
Losses are not going to happen very often to the extent that they occurred in 1951. Very few dollars have come out of P.F.A.A. into the area that I have in mind with the exception of the year 1951, when devastating hailstorms struck the area. I do not know what the department may feel able to do, but I do think that consideration should be given to allowing barley to be used to determine the

eligibility in that mixed farming area and, secondly, I think there ought to be some consideration given to the idea of decreasing the size of the block on which payments may be made as a result of loss by hail.
I wonder if the minister has figures showing the amounts collected in 1951 and 1952 as the result of the 1 per cent levy on grain cheques?
For what years?

In 1950-51 the total collected was $7,334,059.06. In 1951-52 the total was $8,967,076.24. I might say that the total amount collected since the act was passed is $69,325,954.54 and the total amount of payments over that period of time is $143,327,607.65. The payments for 1950 were $10,485,000 and for 1951 they were $4,505,000. Payments are not complete for 1952.
Thank you.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to address a few comments on this item because irrigation has become an important farm factor on Vancouver island. I make no apologies for speaking at this time because provision of adequate supplies of water is just as essential to the farmers on Vancouver island as to the farmers in any other part of the country. The southern portion of the island in particular is very dry and while the average rainfall in Saanich peninsula is about 30 inches during the year, 75 per cent of that rainfall occurs in the six-month period from October to March. Rainfall for the months of April to September in 1951, for example, was 4-63 inches. During the summer season evaporation is heavy, averaging 22 [DOT] 04 inches of water from a free water surface. Furthermore, the rock surface is very close to the top of the soil. Those figures alone indicate the need for irrigation and soil moisture.
Competent authority has estimated that some 20,000 acres of arable land in the Saanich peninsula would lend themselves to irrigation. Unfortunately the supply of water for irrigation in that area is not plentiful. We have no rivers and few lakes in the area that could be used for irrigation purposes. However, in recent years many growers have constructed dugouts, dammed small creeks and dug wells for irrigation purposes. In such cases the water thus conserved has been used for the irrigation of high-priced crops having low water requirement.
Supply-Agriculture
Where water has been made available for irrigation, a great variety of crops have been grown. These range from pastures to vegetable crops, potatoes, tree and small fruits, bulbs, vegetable and flower seed crops. Experience has indicated that with irrigation the increase in production varies from 25 per cent to 100 per cent.
I should like to give a few examples of the difference between crops grown on irrigated and non-irrigated land. These figures were obtained from a report by the dominion experimental station at Saanichton, on irrigation experiments conducted in 1951. On irrigated land, loganberries yielded 6,640 pounds per acre, whereas on non-irrigated land they yielded only 2,232 pounds. On irrigated land raspberries yielded 7-09 tons per acre, whereas on non-irrigated land no marketable yield was obtained. On irrigated land potatoes yielded 19-5 tons per acre, and on non-irrigated land only 4-7 tons. Bulbs, such a daffodils, on irrigated land yielded 50,820 bulbs per acre, whereas on non-irrigated land only 19,965 bulbs per acre were harvested. Gladioli, on irrigated land, yielded 133,856 grade 1 flowers per acre, and on non-irrigated land only 12,705 flowers per acre.
I think those few examples will show how beneficial irrigation can be to the growers on the Saanich peninsula. The total yield is merely a guide to the merits of irrigation, but if the grade and quality of the products are also taken into consideration one sees how very important it is that adequate supplies of water be made available. If the water is correctly applied, as was the case in the tests which were carried out at the experimental farm, the amount of water which should be applied to the growing crops at various times averages from about 4 inches for early maturing crops such as over-wintered vegetable crops and bulbs, to the much larger quantity of about 15 inches for pasture land.
While there is very little fresh water available for irrigation purposes on the Saanich peninsula, that peninsula is practically surrounded by salt water. I feel that if plants could talk they would quote the ancient mariner who said:
Water, water, everywhere,
Nor any drop to drink.
Untreated sea water, of course, is unfit for irrigation purposes because it contains a higher percentage of salt than the plant life can handle. But the salt can be removed from sea water by various methods of distillation. I believe the most modern method is one of vapour compression distillation, developed by

Supply-Agriculture
the Cleaver-Brooks Company of Milwaukee. This is a system of evaporation by thermocompression distillation equipment, and it has many advantages, both practical and economical, as compared with the older method. The theory is based on the fact that evaporation and condensation are, of course, reversible processes. Vapour can be produced from a specific amount of water by adding heat. This package of heat is known as "the latent heat of evaporation". Likewise, when heat is removed from the vapour the process of condensation is established again and the vapour once more becomes water.
Now, since the distillation of sea water is a world-wide problem, hundreds of installations, with units ranging in capacity from 85 to 2,100 gallons per hour, are today producing fresh water from brackish or sea water. They are located on ocean islands, airfields, oil fields, canneries and municipalities throughout the world, wherever there is a lack of pure water for drinking and domestic purposes. The initial investment cost for large units is high, but the operating cost is not very great. The figures I have show that operating costs run from $1.50 to $2 for each 1,000 gallons produced.
So far as I know the production of water for irrigation purposes from the distillation of sea water has not yet been attempted, although investigations and inquiries have been made. However, should a method be developed that would prove feasible, the resultant reclamation of insular and coastal land would undoubtedly be of considerable economic importance. I would therefore ask the minister whether any experiments have been carried out by the scientists of his department, or whether any request has been made of the scientists at the national research council to study this problem. I believe it is a problem which is capable of solution, and for which I am confident a solution will be found before many years have passed. I would hope that Canada would be able to play a leading part in the solution of this problem, and thus make the vast amount of salt water available for irrigation purposes in these coastal regions in which there is no adequate supply of fresh water.
The farmers of Saanich peninsula do need assistance in this matter. I believe that if experiments could be followed out, the solution might well be within sight. I am not going to project my thoughts too far into the future, but it might be that atomic energy would be able to supply the heat element which would be required for the evaporation and condensation of salt water in order to remove the salt.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member for the trouble he has taken in bringing together the thoughts of a great many with regard to this matter of converting salt water into something that could be utilized both for human consumption and for the irrigation of lands along the coast line. I think it is true that practically every country that has been a seafaring country or which borders upon the sea has been experimenting for a long time. We have had the advantage of all publications in connection with it, and our people have been working on it; but I would expect that if a solution is found, while we may be lucky enough to find it, it is more apt to be found in some of the places where they have been concentrating on the question.
With respect to the other matter of irrigating that particular section of the Saanich, as the hon. member pointed out, we have an illustration station there. Some very valuable work is being done on it. One of the most valuable is the demonstrations that are given of the possibilities of sprinkler irrigation, and the people around there are taking it up as far as possible. I understand that the amount of fresh water available is rather limited, and probably one of the high costs is getting it from where it is to where people want to use it; but to the extent they can do that, they do benefit from the experiments that we are carrying on at the experimental station there.
I can assure the hon. member that everything we can do will be done, and all the help we can give will be given in connection with it.

49.	Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, $2,492,285.

I believe that valuable reclamation work is being done in some of these marshlands. I received a letter from the maritimes just recently in which it was indicated that a number of the dikes that had been constructed had been washed out. Is there anything to that? How much damage has been done, or has any damage been done by the tides to the dikes that have been constructed down there?

None of them has been washed out. My information is that these new dikes built by the new methods-perhaps that is a better way of putting it-have stood up much better than we had ever expected, and better than those that had been built a considerable time ago. But of course one could not say that any structures that are near the sea do not suffer any damage from any storm or any extra high tide that comes in, and the tides are very high down there. These storms and high tides are likely to

do damage that was not expected, but there has not been any washing out of the dikes.
How much money has been spent on repairing in the last year?

I cannot get the figures broken down in the way the question was asked, but the grand total that has been spent is $4,142,975. The nearest approach I can get to what the hon. member asked is that in Nova Scotia $1,429,505 has been spent in the four years, in New Brunswick $1,111,530 and in Prince Edward Island, $19,440. There is only one comparatively small project there. These are the expenditures made.
These are the expenditures, but surely that amount was not spent for repairs and maintenance. What I ask is what has been spent on repairs and maintenance?

That is all. These lands were all diked by the French or the British away back a hundred years ago, and the dikes have stood up until very recently. They are built back a certain distance from the sea. The sea has gradually worked underneath them, undermined them in some places, and they have fallen into the sea. We are reconstructing those dikes and opening up that land again.
What I was trying to get at was the amount that had been spent on repairs and maintenance of the new construction that has taken place over the last few years.

Scarcely anything has been spent on them yet. We have done the same thing the original builders did. We have gone back rods from the sea, and we have put up new dikes. Perhaps some day the water will get up close to them and undermine them, too, but it is not going to happen for some considerable time. The amount of damage that has been done has been comparatively small.

I should like to ask one or two questions on this item, particularly with reference to the report on conservation and flood control on the Assiniboine river which was submitted to the department in December, 1952. This report deals particularly with the problem of flooding in the city of Winnipeg. The investigation arose as a result of the disastrous flooding of 1950 in the city of Winnipeg, which as all hon. members know was declared a national emergency. As the minister well knows, the Assiniboine river enters into this problem because it is one of the main tributaries of the Red river.
In conjunction with the diking and flood control on the Assiniboine river, we have the problem of flooding between Millwood and Brandon. This particular subject was discussed at some length in the report to which I have already referred. Can the minister make any comment on the present thinking of the government in regard to that particular problem?
May I revert once again to the other matter which is covered particularly by the estimate indicated on page 7. Last year we had a discussion on the diking operations taking place in the Portage area. This year the amount is being doubled, from $50,000 to $100,000. I am wondering whether that is to apply exclusively to that area, or whether the sum of money will be available for the broader problem of flooding on the Assiniboine river.
Then a final question. The proposition was put forward in the conservation and flood control report to the effect that the cut-off at Portage should be combined with the Russell reservoir project. It is intimated that if the Russell reservoir project were proceeded with, it would decrease by at least 10 per cent the danger of flooding in the area between Millwood and Brandon. It is further indicated in the report that one project without the other is useless. It has to be a combined effort, that is, both the Portage cutoff and the Russell reservoir. I am interested in discovering just how far the government has gone in its work and thinking along these lines.

Supply-Agriculture

I hold in my hand a report which has not yet been distributed, but it does cover the point just mentioned by the hon. member. I think the best advice I could give him would be to get a copy of the report as soon as it is available, and I am sure that in it he will find answers to everything he has just mentioned. I must say that I have not yet had the opportunity to read it. This investigation was carried on by our people. There has been a survey of the whole Assiniboine river area, beginning up in Saskatchewan and coming right down to the Red river. It is all set out in this volume, which will be available shortly.
Then, on the other question, as the hon. member knows, at the time of the last serious flooding in Brandon I was invited to go out there and look over the market gardens on the north side of the river. I did so. We are just as much interested in those as we are in the problems down around Portage. As I have said on previous occasions, the objective has been to make the Assiniboine river operations just as important as those we have had on the Souris river, or on any of the other rivers, and to carry on those operations all the way from the source of the river right down its whole distance to the Red river.
In three or four municipalities down around Portage we have done work which has resulted in diking and the cutting off of curves in the river in order to allow the water to get away more rapidly than it otherwise would. And at other places upstream we have put in dams in order to prevent the water from coming down as rapidly as it would otherwise. I can assure the hon. member that we are going right ahead with that kind of work, and I would hope that in the years ahead the government will be able to accomplish even more than it has up to now in connection with that activity.
I would conclude from the minister's remarks that this report will be tabled shortly; is that correct?

I am not so sure whether it will be in shape to be tabled before the session closes. It is a report which we must turn over to the Department of Resources and Development, and they will handle it. Our P.F.R.A. people have done the job for that department, because it is partly related to the problem they have down at Winnipeg in connection with the flooding situation.

I have one general question to ask. In view of legislation which has been before the house concerning water conservation, and which was sponsored by the Department of Resources and Development, I am wondering what liaison there

will be where these two interests might overlap, or where action might be taken to the same end.
Does the hon. member mean as between the Department of Resources and Development and the Department of Agriculture?
Yes, on the matter of water conservation.

The difference between the two is this; and I think I could give a better illustration by going out to my own province, where I know the situation better. A suggestion has been made to put a weir in the Saskatchewan river so that it would be of some assistance in the neighbourhood of Prince Albert. The putting of a weir in there would have no relationship to agriculture whatsoever. It would provide landing places for aircraft from the north country, so that they might land in the water.
Facilities would be provided at Prince Albert similar to those at Saskatoon. However, the work at Saskatoon might be said to have some bearing upon agriculture, while the other would not. P.F.R.A. or the Department of Agriculture would not undertake the one at Prince Albert, but we did have something to do with that at Saskatoon. The determining factor is that if there is promotion of agriculture or the conservation of soil, or related matters, it is presumed to be done by the Department of Agriculture either provincially or federally, or by the two in co-operation. But if it is purely a matter of putting up a dam to prevent the flooding of a city, as for example at the city of London, then it is done in co-operation between the provincial government and the federal Department of Resources and Development.

There would seem to be some difficulty in some cases in distinguishing between the responsibilities of the respective departments of government. As the minister knows, the flooding of a river is generally caused by the kind of land usage carried on in the watershed of that river. These are closely related subjects in nearly every case, I suggest.
That is correct.

Item agreed to.
SI.	To provide for administrative expenses, Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, $98,592.

This is the same item we have had each year since the support act became effective. I notice, however, in looking over the supplementary estimates for this year that there is no vote such as appeared in the supplementary estimates in the past number of years. The estimate in last year's

supplementaries, numbered 674, was as follows:
Amount required to recoup agricultural prices support account, to cover net operating losses of the agricultural prices support board during the fiscal year 1951-52.
Were there any losses during 1952-1953? If so, what method is the government using to recoup the fund? I notice there is no vote in this year's supplementary estimates.

All the losses up to the end of March, or in the year preceding the end of March in any year, are voted under the further supplementary estimates at that time. The administrative vote, as it is set out here, is about the same every year; there is not much difference in that. We do not know in advance what losses will be taken. As has been said by hon. members on a number of occasions, they have been very small. We had $200 million to work with, and for a considerable number of years we had losses of only $10 million. Our experience this year will be quite different, largely because we had the foot-and-mouth disease and so on. Speaking just from memory, at one time we had $125 million out. Much of that is coming back from day to day, but we will have final losses running into some millions.
How will the fund be recouped? For years it was recouped by means of a vote in the estimates.
The hon. member will recall that the Minister of Finance brought down an item of $32 million in the supplementary estimates. We might have some further losses later on.

I still cannot understand why this does not appear as it has in other years, in the agriculture supplementary estimates. Since the act came into force there has been a vote in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture to recoup the fund. Has there been a change in policy? Why is there not an item in the supplementary estimates under the Department of Agriculture to take care of the recouping of this fund?
I am informed that the anticipated losses for this year were covered by the vote in the supplementary estimates.
Then the fund is being recouped by a vote in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Finance?
Of the Department of Agriculture. They were brought down by the Minister of Finance, as I did not happen to be here at the time. The amount was $32,346,000.

Last year in our area the condensers were taking a large amount of the
Supply-Agriculture
milk produced but a situation has arisen, largely because of the embargo due to the foot-and-mouth disease, whereby large numbers of dairy cattle remain on the farm. I am afraid we are going to run into a surplus of milk in the cheese factories. Would it be possible to channel a certain amount of that milk into other production, such as butter? Has the prices support board considered purchasing cheese should we run into a surplus condition?

The Ontario cheese producers have organized their activities under the agricultural co-operative marketing act, which was passed in 1939. Under that act we are prepared to guarantee up to 80 per cent of the average price for the three preceding years. The Ontario producers had that guarantee last year and I understand are putting forward a request for the same thing this year. Last year the provincial government added six cents. I have no information as to what they intend to do this year, but I think it can be taken for granted that we will pretty well stick to what was done last year. I think it would be a mistake to transfer from the act they are now under to the Agricultural Prices Support Act.

Item agreed to.
52.	To provide for the furnishing of a room in the headquarters building of the food and agriculture organization, Rome, Italy, $10,000.
Is the same thing being done here that is done in case of the Department of External Affairs? I suppose this $10,000 will be expended in the form of blocked currency of the country?
It is our share. All the others are paying for it.
Item agreed to.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this time I wish to make a statement that was foreshadowed in the speech from the throne, and I now do so on the opening of the department's estimates.
The house knows the government's basic health objective, of course, to bring the best of health care within reach of every Canadian. A few days from now we will reach the fifth anniversary of the national health program, the symbol and centre of recent health progress in this country. When the late prime minister, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, introduced this program in 1948, he placed it in proper perspective in relation to the government's larger and basic aim of securing for the people of Canada a national minimum of social security and human welfare. In so doing he pointed out that the new federal grants represented "first stages in the development of a comprehensive health insurance plan for all Canada".
Nothing could better mark the success of this program over its first five years than the government's decision, which I have the honour of announcing today, to move forward on three entirely new health fronts. The house will be asked to approve the addition of three important federal health grants to the ten already in existence.
These new grants will give invaluable aid to the provinces in providing: (1) better health care for mothers and children; (2) better health care for the disabled, and (3) better facilities and services to help doctors diagnose their patients' illnesses. This threefold federal program, when fully developed, will total almost $11 million each year.
These new grants take full account of the health surveys made by the provinces with federal aid. In developing them we have worked closely with provincial public health leaders, with representatives of the health professions and with the various voluntary associations. Meetings have already been held with senior health officials in the provinces so that no time will be lost in getting these new programs under way as soon as the necessary appropriations are approved by

parliament. As members of the house know, the provinces, after assessing their needs in each field covered by federal grants, submit projects which are then studied and, if acceptable, approved by the federal government.
But it is not just projects and administrative procedures that these new grants should bring to our minds. Rather our thoughts should be of births unmarred by the death of mother or child, of broken bodies brought back to useful activity, of countless Canadians helped in their fight for good health because, through the great techniques of modern medical

I now turn to a more detailed review of each of these new grants, and first I shall deal with the child and maternal health grant. A grant of $2 million is proposed to help provide better health services for Canada's mothers and children. This grant, which will start this year at $500,000 and double next pear and the year after, will be distributed m the basis of a flat amount of $10,000 to sach province, with the balance divided among the provinces according to the num-ler of births and infant deaths.
At the present time the level of health services for mothers and children varies :onsiderably from province to province and ;ven within provinces. We want to see these :ssential services more uniformly developed across Canada. We want to make sure that, is far as possible, every Canadian mother :an have access to proper health care before, luring and after the birth of her child.

In summary, over the next five years these three new grants-to give them their official names, child and maternal health, medical rehabilitation, and laboratory and radiological services-will make $42 million available for an expanded health program. and maternal health; better educational services for expectant mothers; more medical research on pregnancy; improved equipment for maternity wards in hospitals; more services for mothers and children in hospital outpatient departments and community health centres.
In short, through this new grant more Canadian infants will be able to get a healthy start in life and more Canadian mothers will be able to bear children without danger to their own health. The vital significance of this grant is realized when we recall that this year's births will involve the life and health of 800,000 Canadian infants and their mothers.
Now, Mr. Chairman, while this is the first time a particular grant has been given for maternal and child health, substantial assistance in this field has already been provided through other sections of the federal health program. There can be no question that this federal aid over the past five years has been a factor in the decline in infant deaths in Canada from 16,333 in 1947 to 14,584 in 1951, a total saving of 10,000 infant lives in this period.
During the past eight years we have also done a great deal through family allowances to provide more equal opportunity for our children through their infancy and up through the years of childhood and adolescence. But despite our provisions for the health and wellbeing of our children, we find that the Canadian infant death rate is still too far above the level of certain other countries whose economic capacity and social development are, in other respects, no greater than our own! This new grant will help provide Canadian mothers and children with the health services

Supply-Health and Welfare of modern medical science. No proposal of this government, I know, could appeal more tellingly to the hearts and minds of the people of this country.
The second of the new health grants, the rehabilitation services grant, is intended to provide improved health services for our disabled citizens. In recent years the federal government has taken an increasing interest in the problem of the disabled. Our programs for disabled veterans rank with the best in the world. The Department of Labour, through the federal employment service, makes special efforts to place handicapped persons in useful, productive and satisfying employment. The national health program itself has benefited thousands of crippled children and those recovering from tuberculosis, mental illness, arthritis and polio. The hospital construction grant has helped to set up rehabilitation centres such as the western society for physical rehabilitation in Vancouver.
The purpose of this new grant is to fill the gaps in existing programs, to help develop suitable services for handicapped persons not already provided for by government or voluntary agencies. I have in mind such persons as those who have had legs or arms amputated, the paraplegics, victims of accidents for whom there is no other provision, and all those suffering from the many disabling conditions which can cripple the human body and so tragically restrict the creative capacity of the human spirit.
A special grant of this sort was proposed in February, 1952, by the newly-established national advisory committee on rehabilitation. This body, appointed by the federal government and representing all provincial governments, the medical and allied professions, the voluntary agencies, organized labour, management and the universities, was a direct outgrowth of a conference convened jointly the year before by my colleagues the ministers of labour and veterans affairs, and myself.
Disability, as we were reminded by the hon. member for Fort William who spoke on this subject a few months ago, is not a simple condition to be countered by any single program. There are many types of disability, and there are many aspects to the rehabilitation process if the disabled person is to be effectively led back to a useful and productive life. This grant will be for services that will help restore the health of the disabled person and reduce his disability to a minimum. These activities will be closely co-ordinated with the vocational training and special placement programs of the Department of Labour.
This grant for the disabled will total $1 million a year-for the first year it will be

one-half this amount. There will be $10,000 a year for each province, with the balance divided on the basis of population. Each project approved under this grant must fit into our over-all program to help our disabled citizens. Otherwise a haphazard pattern might develop, with a single service provided here, some equipment set up there, but no thought for our final objective which is to help as many disabled persons as possible take an active and satisfying part in the life of their community.
Funds available under this grant will be used for three main purposes: (1) for the training of professional rehabilitation workers; (2) for medical rehabilitation equipment; and (3) for rehabilitation health services. Training might be for any of the professional health and welfare workers who can help the disabled, including physicians, psychiatrists, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, social workers, nurses, remedial gymnasts and rehabilitation officers. Equipment could include electrotherapy apparatus, Hubbard baths, whirlpool baths, remedial gymnastic apparatus and other special equipment used to correct disabilities.
In the extension of services, this grant could help employ the necessary professional staff for hospitals and rehabilitation centres. It could also be used to finance surveys to seek out persons with disabilities, to set up units where crippled persons could get help with their appliances, and to set up other specialized clinics and units essential in any well-balanced program for the disabled.
While training and equipment projects can be financed entirely out of federal funds under this grant, the provinces must share equally in the cost of extending services. This grant is not intended to make rehabilitation a federal field of action, but rather to assist the provinces in meeting what is basically their responsibility. It will also give encouragement to the many voluntary agencies already doing splendid work in this field. I am aware that my mere recital cannot bring home immediately the significance of this grant, but all one has to do is visit any part of this country and learn of the work being done, and one will at once realize the significance of this grant in connection with that work.
I come now to the last, the largest and, in many ways, the most significant of the new grants here proposed, that for the extension of laboratory and radiological services. This grant will make possible better health care for Canadians by providing their physicians with better facilities and services to detect disease and ill health with consequential benefit and great service to the

people as a whole. Starting at 30 cents per capita, this grant will rise by 5 cents each year to a maximum of 50 cents per capita in the fifth and succeeding years. In general, the provinces will match dollar for dollar the federal funds made available. This grant will total approximately $4,300,000 this year, rising over the next five years to about $7,800,000. The per capita allotment will then remain unchanged, but the grant will, of course, continue to increase year by year as our population increases.
The importance of this new grant will at once be evident to every member of this house. It represents the fulfilment of an objective which the former prime minister in announcing this program placed before the house, and one which I have repeatedly placed before this house and the country during the past five years. This is what we had in mind, as I stated, when I made my first report on the national health program to the Canadian Medical Association shortly after it was announced. As I said then:
The black bag is still the symbol of the medical profession, but the discerning doctor must see himself and his services against the broad pattern of medical facilities that the Canadian community has developed to enable him to serve it better. The history of medicine reflects the growing dependence of the doctor on the health facilities available to him. To the simple relationship between doctor and patient have been added the diagnostic, hospital, laboratory and other facilities that have been developed to support the doctor in his work.
We must make sure now that our people in all parts of the country are not denied these diagnostic facilities, now not fully the case. Much has already been done, of course, under the hospital construction grant to develop more adequate hospital facilities and, under the other grants, to extend the diagnostic and laboratory facilities our doctors require to serve their patients effectively. This new grant, however, makes possible an expanded program for the setting up of modern diagnostic facilities, particularly in rural areas where they do not now exist, as well as in some other communities.
We have expanded the capacity of our hospitals; we now propose to give them more help in establishing X-ray and other diagnostic services under medically competent personnel. Health authorities recognize the importance of providing this specialized service to the medical practitioner so that he can better serve the people under his care. The health surveys made by the provinces, under the national health program and at federal expense entirely, indicate a fundamental need to extend diagnostic facilities and services so that people in all parts o Canada may have more ready access to the 68108-296
Supply-Health and Welfare high quality of medical care now generally available in our cities.
Since these specialized facilities are relatively expensive to establish and of a very technical nature, they cannot easily be provided by the practising physician himself. Through this grant it will be possible to set up services where needed in hospitals and health centres to meet the requirements of doctors and patients in the areas concerned. By improving the facilities now available to private practitioners for the diagnosis of illness outside of hospital, this grant is expected to reduce the need for additional hospital accommodation. By making laboratory and X-ray facilities and services more widely available, particularly in outlying areas, it will cut down the time and money spent in travelling to the larger medical centres.
Of particular importance will be the better distribution of medical personnel throughout Canada that should result from this grant. One of the major reasons more doctors do not settle in certain areas is that facilities are so frequently lacking for the practice of the kind of medicine they are taught in medical schools today. This problem can, in part, be solved by the judicious extension of laboratory, X-ray and other diagnostic facilities and services to supplement those already in existence in the smaller hospitals.
Finally, the grant should help facilitate the training of radiologists, more and more becoming an increasingly important factor in the great work that is being done by those who have to do with the health of our people. In this connection, the greatest care will be taken to ensure that the training provided is of the highest standard.
Provincial projects under this grant will be devoted primarily to the development of improved facilities in those areas that are not now adequately served. There is no thought of duplicating existing services if they are performing a useful and economical function. The services now provided by the major laboratories and in the larger hospitals and universities are second to none. Much splendid work is also being done by the various provincial diagnostic services. Through this new grant it is our hope to continue to encourage accuracy and quality in order that physicians, in all parts of Canada, may have complete confidence in the reports made to them.
As hon. members know, we have already given substantial assistance toward the provision of X-ray services through the cancer and tuberculosis control grants. Our purpose now is not, of course, to duplicate what has

Supply-Health and Welfare been, done but rather to extend facilities for the early diagnosis of fracture, of chest and abdominal ailments, and for other X-ray procedures required in the physician's work. In the laboratory field, encouragement will be given to the development of modern facilities staffed and supervised by specially trained workers capable of giving to all physicians and patients the kind of expert help they now receive in the leading hospitals in large urban centres. These laboratory services include such procedures as electrocardiograms, so necessary to modern heart investigation, and basal metabolism tests for glandular treatment.
Let me stress the importance in all these developments of maintaining the traditional doctor-patient relationship. There is no thought of regimentation or centralization of personal health services. We do not want to see in Canada any barrier imposed between doctor and patient, for that would lessen the doctor's effectiveness and the patient would inevitably suffer. The purpose of this grant is rather to strengthen the physician's hand, since he is most immediately responsible for the health of the patient. In that way we hope to bring greater and more direct assistance to the people themselves.
Now, the greatest care must be taken to see that nothing is permitted to lower the high standards of medical practice for which Canada has won world-wide recognition. We must remember that it is not the function of a public health service to carry out personal health services that are properly the responsibility of the private practising physician. This grant will enable the private physician to serve his patients better. I was told only this morning by a country doctor who lives some 600 miles away, who came down to see me and with whom I discussed some of the phases of this program without revealing government policy, that in his judgment this was the greatest step yet taken to assist those in outside areas in getting this kind of investigatory treatment and attention. I am sure that will be the verdict of this house, and I know it will be the verdict of this country. This grant will help to bring the latest techniques of medical science into the service of the whole Canadian people.
These three new grants that I have outlined are logical extensions of the national health program. They were decided upon only after the greatest consideration and in the light of our wide experience in bridging the gaps in Canada's health services. The house will be interested to learn that because of our remarkable progress in building new hospitals since 1948, we now find it possible

to embark on these programs without imposing a further burden on the taxpayer. We are now able to divert about half of the hospital construction grant to offset, in large part, the additional expenditures proposed, and yet keep toward the objective established for ourselves five years ago.
Many hon. members now present were in this house on that historic day, May 14, 1948, when the late prime minister announced the inauguration of Canada's national health program. Mr. King pointed out that besides being fundamental prerequisites of a nationwide system of health insurance, these substantial grants-undertaken at federal initiative and extending considerably beyond the 1945-46 proposals to the provinces- opened a new era in health for Canada. Let us see if his words on that date have been confirmed by experience in the intervening years.
During the first five years of this program the provinces have been able to expend $100 million or 60 per cent of the more than $165 million in federal funds made available to them for the following broad purposes: to survey their own health programs and future needs; to help overcome serious shortages in hospital accommodation; to raise the level of training of health workers and to encourage health research; to improve public health facilities and services in rural and urban Canada; and, finally, to intensify efforts to combat crippling conditions in children, venereal disease, mental illness, rheumatism and arthritis, tuberculosis and cancer.
The effect of this transfusion of federal funds into the bloodstream of provincial health services is literally incalculable and staggering in its results, as I propose now to show. Its influence has been felt throughout every part of Canada. I am sure every hon. member can testify from personal knowledge to the practical, tangible benefits which these federal health grants have brought to those he represents in this parliament, and I am conscious of the fact that in speaking of the health of the people, I am talking about something which, in the words of Benjamin Disraeli, the prime minister of Queen Victoria, represents the greatest asset of any nation.
If it were possible to trace its effect on individual Canadians over the past five years, it would be clear that the national health program has directly touched the lives of fully 75 per cent of our people and, more indirectly, of all Canadians.
The other day a member of this house asked me for some facts and figures on expenditures under this program. I gave

him this information, but what I perhaps should have told him was that the program's achievements cannot be measured in dollars and cents, impressive though these figures are, but in their effect on the health and well-being of our people. I only wish I could have taken him into the highways and byways of Canada and shown him at firsthand some of the inspiring new developments that are taking place because of this great federal program, that will stand as a monument to a great humanitarian prime minister, the late Mr. Mackenzie King.
Let me briefly indicate the scope of this outstanding social measure by listing some of the achievements made possible by federal expenditures under it. Through these federal grants 8,600,000 people, 60 per cent of our entire population, are now served by health units. I ask hon. members just to think of what that in itself means. Through these federal grants 2 million free chest X-ray examinations are given each year. Go into the office of any radiologist or any doctor, or ask any doctor of this house what these X-rays have shown not only by way of revealing tubercular conditions, positive and negative, but by way of revealing and checking other illnesses which would not have been known and which would never have been uncovered unless this service had been made possible by this program, in collaboration with the provincial governments.
Through these federal grants hospital facilities have been established for the first time in 144 communities across Canada; 5,000 health workers have been trained, and more than 4,600 have been added to hospital staffs and other health services. More than
1.200.000	children have benefited through improved health services. In place of 17, there are now 77 mental health clinics where
12.000	Canadians, many of them children, are receiving help. Through these grants 25,000 tuberculosis patients have been provided with streptomycin and other drugs free of charge, and 500,000 infants have been given B.C.G. protection against tuberculosis.
The reason we have provided these drugs free is not that we want to give anything for nothing. We give these drugs to patients in sanatoria in an effort to bring about a reduction in this dreaded disease. It is a costly drug, and only in that way could we have had a uniform practice; and the results, as I shall indicate, have been simply stupendous. Through these grants cancer diagnostic services have been provided to more than 100,000 persons. I am sure the committee will appreciate why I speak with fervour, conviction and with emphasis. I 68108-296i
Supply-Health and Welfare think it is something to be able to say that one is administering a program which has resulted in providing cancer diagnostic services to more than 100,000 people in Canada.
One of the most striking achievements has been the government's leadership in providing additional hospital accommodation, which has been increased by 46,000 beds since 1948, a rate of hospital building never before approached in our history. We have built through this assistance, and with provincial assistance and with voluntary effort primarily, in the past four and a half years one-third as many hospital beds as were in existence in Canada on May 14, 1948.
The new appropriation for hospital construction during 1953-54 amounting to $6,850,000 will be supplemented by a carryover, bringing the total amount available for the coming year to some $20 million. Over the next five years, total allocations will equal or exceed actual expenditures made under this grant since the beginning of the program.
When this program was announced we said we were going to try to see that
40,000	hospital beds were provided in Canada in a five-year period. We have exceeded that objective by over 6,000. When Mr. King announced the program he said that at the end of the first five years the program would be reviewed, and that is what we are doing now.
Another striking fact is that in the five-year period covered by the national health program, the death rate from tuberculosis has been cut almost in half. This achievement reflects an established trend reinforced with greatly increased case-finding programs and the use of new and beneficial drugs. The Canadian tuberculosis association informs us that the tuberculosis death rate for 1952 will be under 20 as compared to the rate of 24-5 for 1951.
In this connection, Dr. Louis Dublin, vicepresident of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company and one of the outstanding public health authorities on the North American continent, has this to say of Canada's achievement:
Progress in the fight on tuberculosis is the outstanding feature of the year's health record. The 1952 death rate from the disease is likely to break below 20 per 100,000 population, or a 10 per cent improvement over the previous minimum recorded in 1951. It is hard to realize that only five years ago the rate was double the 1952 estimated figure.
I am not saying that this tremendous achievement in the five years during which the national health program has been in existence is due entirely to this program, but undoubtedly it has been a stimulating factor

Supply-Health and Welfare in bringing about the great results that have been achieved.
I ask the house to consider for a moment the significance of the statement I have just read. What do the statistics mean in terms of lives actually saved? In 1947, the year before the national health program, deaths from tuberculosis in Canada totalled 5,449. Had the 1947 death rate continued into 1951, 6,076 persons would have fallen victim to this scourge, instead of which the actual number of deaths was 3,417. In other words, in 1951 because of the great improvement in our tuberculosis control and treatment measures, 2,659 Canadians escaped death from tuberculosis.
This magnificent achievement would not have been possible had it not been for the wholehearted collaboration of all who joined in the battle against this scourge, whether as federal, provincial or municipal health officers, or professional and voluntary health workers. It is through them that the federal tuberculosis control grant has made its significant contribution in bringing about this almost miraculous saving in human life. Consider just one phase of the federal program. More than $2 million has been made available for the purchase of streptomycin and other life-saving drugs so essential in the modern treatment of tuberculosis. Go and ask the director of any sanatorium today the significance of that.
We can truly be proud of our record but we do not intend to slacken our efforts. The fight must go on. Our objective for the years ahead must be to reduce the numbers of those contracting this disease as rapidly as we have reduced deaths from it. If I may repeat what I said in this house four years ago:
The objective of our tuberculosis program for the next generation is nothing less than the elimination of this disease as a major cause of death and illness among our population.
From what I have said of its success, and from their own personal experience, hon. members who supported the national health program in 1948 have reason to know how fully it has lived up to our high hopes. I am confident that we who are here today will hear similar reports in the years ahead to prove the wisdom of these further steps that we are taking in the development of this country's public health services to provide better health care for Canadian mothers and children, to help our disabled, and to enable our doctors to serve their patients more effectively, and thereby bring lasting benefits to the people as a whole.
These new grants constitute a further and finer stage in the development of Canada's national health program. They represent,

however, no departure from its established pattern. They are consistent with the spirit, the purpose and the objectives of the government's basic policy in the field of public health-stage by stage, to bring the best of health care within reach of every Canadian.
The successful administration of the new grants will call for co-operation and imaginative leadership from Canada's medical profession and from public health officials at every level of organization. Through its program and the extensions that I have set before the house today, the government is proud to have the honour of implementing new services that will enable Canada's health workers to maintain and add to their distinguished tradition. In this, in Pasteur's words, "by obeying the laws of humanity, they will be extending the frontiers of life."
This expanded program stands as a further testimony to this government's belief that in health, as in so many other fields, the public interest is best served by steady, responsible, forward-looking measures timed so that we can consolidate our gains as we go along. A very distinguished medical authority in the United States, Dr. J. H. Means, for many years professor of medicine at Harvard university, writing recently in the Atlantic Monthly, said this about the extension of Canada's federal health program as projected in the throne speech:
It appears that nation-wide searching for better ways to bring health to all the people, particularly with reference to the role of government therein, is far more in evidence in Canada than it is in our own country.
By any standard, Canada's public health achievements merit respect. But the orderly progress of our health plans seems all the more remarkable when considered against the sombre background of a world in turmoil. Concern for the health of the citizen is one of the surest marks of an enlightened society. We know that when the programs for our people are weighed before the world, there is convincing evidence of our genuine and humanitarian concern for the welfare of every Canadian.
It is in that spirit that these further advances are now made possible. As long as peace safeguards our progress, measures such as these are. symbols of that continuing and wholehearted collaboration between Canada's public and private health workers that, with the steady support of our people, is bringing us ever nearer our common objective, the highest possible standard of health for all Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, in our time Canadian governments and Canadian parliaments have enacted many historic and far-reaching pieces

4G87
of social legislation. But I believe that when other legislators, of other generations, look back across the panorama of these years, the national health program will stand enduringly as one of the finest monuments to the humanity of this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has introduced new and additional grants in connection with the health program amounting to some $11 million. I remember very well in May, 1948, when the then prime minister introduced the other health grants, and I remember the reaction at that time, when we took the attitude that money spent for any purpose so far as health was concerned was money well spent. I have never felt in the House of Commons that we could get sufficient money to advance the projects we had in mind in order that disease and suffering might be cut down.
In May of 1948 we voted gladly for those grants, as we will for these. Three items in the grants the minister has introduced today are items we have suggested in some way or other in the house, although perhaps not just as he has put them down. We have felt, for instance, that in addition to a maternal health grant, something should be done to cut down the mortality rate from children's diseases, as well as the infant mortality rate. I can remember on several occasions criticizing the infant mortality percentage, and saying that something should be done about it. On those occasions I have compared our infant mortality rate with that in the United States. I have never been able to understand why our rate should be so much higher than that in the great country to the south of us.
The introduction today of this grant of $2 million will go a long way toward cutting down that mortality rate. With that grant, which I presume is confined to infants and would not apply to children of greater age, is coupled the fact that there will be a grant to cut down the rate of maternal mortality. We have had some experience with that in Ontario, and I can remember well the good that was done when that work was undertaken. During the time the present Leader of the Opposition was premier of Ontario, a series of grants was introduced under which every pregnant mother in the province was entitled to one free and complete examination. I felt that that went a long way to cut down both maternal and infant mortality. I have spoken in this house about the number of premature infants who died, and indicated that I thought the rate was unduly high. Grants of this kind, coupled with the work being done already in the provinces,
Supply-Health and Welfare will help considerably. I do not know how much work is being done in other provinces, but I am aware of the activities in Ontario. All this will help to cut down these rates.
Rehabilitation grants for people who have been crippled are something with which I fully agree. I have not time to fully cover all the minister's statement. I tried to follow him as he made it, but I should like to study it further. As we go along with the different items we will be asking questions of the minister.
Dealing again with what is done in my own province, I can say that money spent for purposes of this kind is money well spent. Some years ago Ontario initiated a plan under which any child that developed poliomyelitis was given free treatment. This saved many children from crippling. As physicians we did not have the ability or the means to adequately treat many of these polio cases. We did not understand the causes and we knew very little about the treatment.
Certain hospitals within the province were set up as treatment centres. When a child entered one of these centres he was under the care of doctors who knew as much as we could possibly know at that time about polio. Advanced treatment was given so far as physiotherapy was concerned, or even surgery. The province paid all bills while the child was under treatment with the exception of the transportation to the selected hospital centre.
I can remember very well patients who were given this treatment. I remember once a patient who received treatment at the Ottawa Civic Hospital and who now shows little or no signs of what in the old days would have been complete paralysis. As I say, money spent in this way is money well spent. Possibly because of my profession I cannot help but agree with this expenditure. I will always try to get all the money possible in the cause of public health, so long as it is properly and well expended.
I come now to the rehabilitation grants for invalids. Some time ago we had a debate in this house on pensions for disabled people. I have had some experience in the rehabilitation of disabled persons through watching the work done by service clubs throughout the country, who collect funds to be expended in this way. There are also other voluntary agencies carrying on this work. The results show that the money is exceptionally well spent.
A child may be crippled with no chance of anything being done under ordinary circumstances, but a service club may arrange

Supply-Health and Welfare to have the child taken to a hospital and given the best and most up to date orthopedic surgery. That child may be returned to his family as a useful member with little or no crippling. A grant for this purpose cannot be criticized, and I am sure the crippled children's society of Ontario and the service clubs will be glad that recognition is being given to the work that is being done in an attempt to rehabilitate people of this sort and allow them to take a useful place in society.
I was not completely convinced after the debate on pensions for disabled persons. I realize that we should be glad for what we are getting, but I still feel that something should be done for the person who does not respond to rehabilitation treatment. I think if the minister made a survey he would find some of these people in every area of Canada. It is rather difficult for their family and the municipality in which they live to deal with this matter. They are not eligible for pension and I make an appeal to the government to close this gap. Under existing legislation all they can look forward to at the present time if they are completely crippled is the time when they will be 65 years of age and be eligible for pension. I am glad that something is being done to rehabilitate people, but I submit that there should be an extension of pensions under the welfare branch of the minister's department to take care of this group.
The extension of laboratory and radiological service will be of great assistance. I am aware of the work being done by certain volunteer agencies in Ontario. I know of one service club which deals entirely with tuberculosis control work. They raise funds every year for this purpose, and if a person in the area cannot afford it, he is sent to a hospital where he gets a free X-ray.
Hon. members may be aware of the mass X-raying that has been carried out by the province of Ontario. I know what was done in my home town. Every person could go and have an X-ray taken. Industries were entitled to send all their employees. Fortunately the percentage of active cases of tuberculosis is becoming steadily less and less, but it is amazing the number of other conditions that are found when these X-rays are taken.
The extension of laboratory services is filling a long-felt want, because doctors will find this of marked benefit in the diagnosis of disease. When the minister mentioned electrocardiograms I could not help but think of the difficulty doctors in many outlying districts have in getting an electrocardiogram.
