AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE Department-
249. Departmental administration, $1,001,677.

When the committee rose for dinner at six o'clock I was discussing the matter of diagnostic facilities under the increased grants. I think this is very important because diagnostic centres will bring the possibility of better diagnosis nearer to certain elements of the population, especially in rural districts. I think that is one good way of approaching this question. But there is also another matter which we must consider at the present time; that is our ageing population, and also the fact that it is inevitable that our aged people will die of some cause. Very often it will be a degenerative disease of some kind. It may be a cerebral accident or heart disease or it may be cancer, because according to our statistics better diagnosis may increase the number of cases of cancer. But these cases will occur in our aged population.
A diagnostic centre with X-ray facilities will enable doctors to make early diagnoses which is the main point in so far as cutting down the number of people who die of cancer is concerned. I am not sure what the statistics for last year show, but approximately 16,000 people in Canada die of cancer every year. Even with respect to our younger population there will be an opportunity in a diagnostic centre to make an early diagnosis in order

that some form of treatment known to us may cut down the mortality rate.
There is one other question that I want to bring up at the present time which has to do with the amount allotted for research. Having regard to causes of death in the Dominion of Canada, I should like to refer to the number of people who are dying from heart disease. I know there has been a discussion among medical men in the city of Toronto about the question of what can be done with respect to sudden deaths from coronary thrombosis. Certainly there is need for our research people to find out what is causing death by coronary sclerosis among many of our younger population. We sometimes expect our older people to die of a heart condition, but the sudden deaths of prominent businessmen in every walk of life seem to be becoming more common all the time. I hope some of the money that the minister has set aside for research will be devoted to that cause.
There is one other thing I must mention, although it does not apply to the health branch. Dealing with causes of death, we can list them something like this. If you look over the causes of death you will see that cardiovascular disease in some form seems to be the principal cause. Whether it is the heart or due to cerebral accident, that seems to be one of the principal causes. Next is cancer. If I may refer for a minute to another cause of death, I wonder if something could not be done with regard to the number of children who are burned to death during the winter months. Fatalities in northern Ontario a few days ago drew this matter to our attention. Several members of a family died in a fire. Then there is also the increasing number of deaths on our highways. This has nothing to do with the matter the minister has introduced today, but I think it is worthy of consideration by the house. When violent deaths in Canada reach fourth place on the list of causes of death, then it is time we should recognize that fact and see what we can do. It becomes an important matter when violent deaths take fourth place as a cause of death in Canada.
There is another matter that I wish to put before the committee, the question of hospitals, which also has something to do with the grants that were introduced this afternoon. I noticed that the minister listed as one of the most striking achievements of the government the providing of additional hospital accommodation. These were the words of the minister this afternoon:
One of the most striking achievements has been the government's leadership in providing additional hospital accommodation, which has been Increased by 46,000 beds since 1948, a rate of hospital building never before approached in our history.
Supply-Health and Welfare
The minister went on to state:
The new appropriation for hospital construction during 1953-54 amounting to $6,850,000 will be supplemented by a carryover bringing the total amount available for the coming year to some $20 million. Over the next five years total allocations will equal or exceed actual expenditures made under this grant since the beginning of the program.
Five years have elapsed since the health grants were introduced in May, 1948. I would take it from the minister's words that the same amount is going to be granted for hospital expansion in the coming five years as we have had in the past five years.
There is another matter I wish to bring to the attention of the committee. Sometimes the general public do not realize just what this means. I remember very well the day the prime minister brought in the health grants, in May, 1948. He stated definitely that the amount per bed to be given by the dominion would be $1,000 for acute cases and $1,500 for chronic cases, with matching grants from the provinces. Let us look at the position of any municipality contemplating a new hospital structure. Let us assume that they are going to build a 100-bed hospital. I am aware that the cost of construction varies in different districts. It may vary anywhere from $5,000 or $6,000 a bed in one hospital to $18,000 a bed, as happened in one case with which I am familiar.
Let us go part way and assume that hospital construction is going to cost $12,000 a bed, with the services which would have to be included in the cost. I am only taking $12,000 per bed in order to prove my point. If the federal government gives $1,000 a bed for a 100-bed hospital for acute cases-I am assuming all the beds are for acute cases, and they usually are-and the province gives $1,000, the amount received in grants by the municipality would be $200,000. It might be a comparatively small municipality which was contemplating a 100-bed addition, and it would be left with a cost of $1 million. In these days of high cost of living, high taxation and so on, municipalities find it difficult to finance hospitals. There is no doubt about that; and any municipality with an additional cost of $1 million is facing a financial problem. The allotment of money for necessary public utilities and that sort of thing, together with the obligation of the municipality toward the hospital, have a tendency to increase taxation. Also there would be a certain amount to be provided through voluntary work and, in these days, it is doubtful if the voluntary appeal can go very much farther. The amount people are asked to donate for such purposes has almost reached the limit.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I want to make this clear. Sometimes I have criticized the minister for the publicity -I call it publicity-put out by his department, when they make the statement that there is a federal grant for hospitals. We are very glad of the grants and I have approved of them; but every time I see one of those statements, and when I see the large headlines, I think of the amount of money the municipality and the taxpayers have to produce. I am bringing this to the attention of the minister, although I have spoken of it before, in order that we may be fair about this thing, and let us have honour where honour is due.
When the late Mr. King introduced these grants he was very clear in his statement. He said, "We will give $1,000 for acute beds, $1,500 for chronic beds and the remainder must be found from other sources". He was very plain. I suggest that in future when grants are announced the department or the minister should keep in mind the statement of the late prime minister when he said the remainder would have to be found from other sources.
I think the three grants announced today constitute a good approach to this question, and I approve of those grants. As I said before, I have always asked for and hoped that there would be additional money for health purposes. I do not think any member in this house can criticize any expenditures in that direction because death, disease, misery and suffering are things beyond this house for which we should raise money if we possibly can. Therefore I can only approve of the grants and say I think they are a step in the proper direction.
While I approve of the grants I want to make a comment on another question. It is the matter of the present position of hospitals as far as accommodation is concerned. Any person who has had any experience knows that hospital boards are having a great deal of difficulty trying to keep on the right side of the ledger. I pay tribute to the hospital boards that are working so hard in that endeavour. It is difficult to finance a hospital, keep the costs of private and semi-private accommodation down, and at the same time produce public ward accommodation at prices that can be met either by the person who pays for it or by the municipality. The situation nowadays is that the cost of public ward accommodation, with the other necessary services, is more than such accommodation should cost the people who are going into those wards. It is very difficult for them to pay, so there is usually a grant from the provincial government; but that grant, combined with the rate received by the hospital,
[Mr. Blair.l

does not begin to cover the expense of public ward accommodation. Therefore hospital boards are forced to raise the fees for semiprivate and private beds. Another sector of the population, therefore, is put in a rather difficult position. If a patient is critically ill the cost of hospital accommodation, of nursing services, of laboratory services, of X-rays and all the other services of the hospital is more than the ordinary man can stand. It is more than the man in the middle income tax brackets can afford. I have had experience with cases where a man with a sick wife or sick child has been faced with a hospital bill that was just simply beyond anything he could pay.
In addition there is the problem that even with the additional 40,000 beds which have been produced since the inauguration of the health grants, practically every hospital has a waiting list. There is a lack of accommodation for those who are chronically ill, and many of them are chronically ill simply on account of age. You will find them all through hospitals-, occupying beds for months and months. There is no other place for them, and they are taking up beds which normally should be occupied by acute cases. One wonders, when hospitals find it so difficult to find beds for acute cases, why there should not be beds for the chronically ill people elsewhere.
I am bringing the position of our elderly citizens to the attention of the department because we did not solve the condition that exists at the present time when we brought in old age pensions, a measure of which I highly approved. An elderly citizen cannot be accommodated anywhere but in a bed in a hospital which should be used for acute cases.
I note that the minister made a speech, in Montreal I think it was, in which he approved of the idea of people being cared for in their homes. I approve also if it could be done but, at the present time, there is very little opportunity to get help in the home. There is difficulty in getting trained nurses, and sometimes it is a bit more expensive to have the doctor make regular calls at the home, so patients are moved into hospitals. There is also the fact that new forms of treatment have made it necessary for many of these people to be moved into the hospital. So we have this group that we must take care of, people whose illnesses are long, people who suffer from these degenerative diseases over a long period of time.
The $1,500 per bed for chronic hospital patients has not covered the situation throughout the country. The minister would know that if he had people coming in, as most doctors do. What can be done with these

chronic cases? Where can we send them? The doctor knows that the situation in the hospital requires that beds be kept for acute cases, and he cannot find a place where these people can go. In the province of Ontario there are really only two convalescent hospitals. There are some convalescent homes springing up; every town has one or two, and they are doing good work; they are relieving hospitals.
I turn now to the question of mental hospitals. When people get old-and we may someday be among the group-they sometimes suffer from cerebral arteriosclerosis and become forgetful. Those people should not be put in mental hospitals; arrangements should be made in the future for a type of hospital that will take care of people who are chronically ill, who are ill by reason of their age, and for this class of people who may be considered forgetful. The mental hospitals are having a hard time to provide accommodation. The provinces are building mental hospitals as fast as they can but mental illness, unfortunately, is increasing and at the present time there is an acute shortage of beds for people who suffer from mental illness. It is a problem, but we have to face problems; that is why we are here.
The minister mentioned in his statement the matter of cutting down the mortality rates for certain diseases, and I pay tribute to those who are responsible. I want to pay full tribute in this regard to the marvellous job that has been done by the provinces, working with their own finances. I do not think the federal government can claim all the credit for cutting down the mortality rates in connection with a disease like tuberculosis. The grants have been a wonderful help, but something else has happened there. Even if the federal government does give a grant to aid in the provision of certain drugs when they are needed, it is the effects of these drugs that have been, in a large way, responsible for the cutting down of the incidence of tuberculosis. We can proceed, and with the help of the municipalities, the provinces and the grants from the federal government I believe we can go a long way further toward cutting down the mortality rate from tuberculosis. In time I believe this disease should be practically nonexistent within this country.
I leave this matter of hospitals with the minister and the committee, because I believe it is an acute problem. Under present conditions, even with the amount of new hospital construction and the repair and extension of existing institutions, I do not believe we can proceed as fast as the need arises. It is apparent that there is today this need for 68108-297
Supply-Health and Welfare accommodation for chronic patients and elderly patients. I do not believe the need of the elderly patients is entirely covered by the recent legislation providing pensions. It was excellent so far as it went, but it is rather difficult for that type of patient to obtain accommodation.
I have been faced with that problem. I am aware of exactly what is happening. As I stated a little while ago, these chronic cases are taking up beds in the hospitals, causing a shortage of beds for acute cases. This is a situation which one finds principally in the smaller centres, where they are finding it difficult to provide beds. We are on a sort of treadmill in that respect; we do not seem to be getting any place.
All I can say about it is that there is this constant demand. Many times in the course of a month I am asked where accommodation can be found for some elderly person, and not just accommodation by way of a place to live. These elderly people might be considered sick, and there is no place to send them. Sometimes these elderly people are sick by reason of their age. They require not only a place to live, but they require some form of nursing and some form of supervision. Due to the fact that there are more elderly people today, this is becoming a greater problem. I think we should consider this phase of the problem in the next step we take in trying to help our aged citizens.
I agree, sir, with the three grants that were brought in today, and I particularly like the last one. I think the establishment of diagnostic centres is one of the best things we could do. It is going to bring medical diagnosis nearer the people. With a disease like cancer, it is very important that we get an early diagnosis. I approve of the grants.
I do say to the committee that I believe we should do something further for these aged people, because they are becoming a problem and we should deal well with them. We should give them the sort of treatment that is necessary. The provision of beds for mental cases is something we must also keep before us. It is to be hoped that the diagnostic facilities provided by these grants for outpatients might relieve the mental hospitals. However, the matter of hospitalization is something that we must keep in front of us. Possibly the problem of accommodation for acute cases could be resolved if we had some place- to send the chronic cases. The matter of beds for people who are mentally ill, and the matter of early diagnosis in all of these cases is of the utmost importance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the late Mr. King made his announcement concerning the health grants program in the

Supply-Health and Welfare House of Commons on May 14, 1948, we in this group immediately expressed our pleasure that this important step in connection with a national health program for Canada had been taken. Since the speech made this afternoon by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I have been interested in re-reading what was said on that important occasion. Indeed, those of us who were here at the time well remember it. I find that my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, concluded his words of welcome with respect to the announcement that had been made by the then prime minister by saying this, as found at page 3937 of Hansard for May 14, 1948:
-I am glad indeed that the Prime Minister, before he retires from the high office which he has indicated he is to relinquish within a short time, has placed before the House of Commons these proposals looking to measures of health insurance and social security which were foreshadowed when he was elected leader of the Liberal party in 1919 . . .
We have had to wait a long time, but I hope that the foundations now being laid will be regarded merely as such, and that, whoever succeeds the Prime Minister in the high office he now occupies- no matter from which quarter of the house his successor may come within the next two or three years-will build upon those foundations a great structure of social security and health insurance for the people of Canada.
Just as we welcomed the announcement of the health grants program in May, 1948, we welcome most heartily the announcement today that that program is to be extended by the addition of three new grants. I shall have something more to say about these specific grants as I go along, but I wish to indicate that, having done that, I shall make the same point that the member for Rosetown-Biggar made on May 14, 1948, namely that we hope this whole health grants program, including these additional grants, will be regarded as Mr. King regarded them, as but steps toward a complete national health program including health insurance for all the people of Canada.
I want, Mr. Chairman, to give all the praise that is deserved for the health grants program that has been in effect for the past five years. I want to give the minister all the praise he deserves for the announcement of the additional services. I confess, however, that I find myself in a bit of difficulty when I want to give the Minister of National Health and Welfare all the praise he deserves. My difficulty is that he has already given himself ten times more praise than he deserves, and there is no room to pile on any more. He is most capable of making these announcements with everything but the blare of trumpets, and I am not so sure that I did not hear that blare. At any rate, if any type of service deserves the blare of trumpets it is the announcement of progress in connection with our national health program.


The minister indicated this afternoon that three grants are being added to those that have been in effect since 1948. In the first place, he told us of the decision to institute a child and maternal health grant. As the minister said, and as the hon. member for Lanark has pointed out, it is a most welcome grant, and it is in keeping with the plans announced by Mr. King in 1948 for a program which would ensure that future generations of Canadian children would be well born regardless of their financial or economic status. As a matter of fact, it is a grant that should have been included in this list long before this; but we welcome it most heartily as one of the announcements made today.
I was disappointed to hear in almost the first paragraph in connection with that announcement that it is to be on a matching basis. If I heard the minister correctly, I believe he said that the provinces were to be expected to match this grant dollar for dollar. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I think that is one mistake that is being compounded in the government's health program, namely the way in which this idea of matching grants is being carried forward. To me it is inconsistent with the principles that were suggested in the Rowell-Sirois report; it is inconsistent with the principles laid down in the proposals made by the federal government to the provinces in 1945, and it is inconsistent with the principles laid down in Mr. King's speech on May 14, 1948. It sounds very good; it sounds plausible to say that the federal government will make grants to the provinces on a dollar for dollar basis; but in the end what it means is that the provinces where the need is greatest but where they have more limited resources will not get the services they need.
As I say, those who have carefully studied federal-provincial relations throughout the years have made it clear that we need to get away from that matching basis, and I am sorry that it is being carried forward in at least two of the new grants the minister announced this afternoon. Apart from that shortcoming with respect to the child and maternal health grants, it was a most welcome announcement.
Likewise, Mr. Chairman, we welcome the announcement that there is to be a rehabilitation services grant. At this very moment I think I should say that I was glad to note in what the minister said that this is not to be on a dollar for dollar or matching basis. If I heard him correctly, I believe he said it was to be on the basis of $10,000 to each province, and then the remainder of the amount being granted would be distributed amongst the provinces on a population basis.

4S93
I suggest that is much fairer than a dollar for dollar basis.
In my view the hon. member for Lanark made very pertinent comments with regard to this rehabilitation services grant. It is something we should be doing; it will be most welcomed by those who will benefit from it. I am glad to note also what close co-operation or liaison there is among the departments of the federal government, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Labour, and the Department of Veterans Affairs, and also the cooperation and liaison between the federal and provincial authorities.
This is a field in which we should be doing a great deal more than we are. We feel it should be one of the marks of a civilization such as ours, that with respect to those in our midst who are physically handicapped in any way, we should go out of our way to provide them with any rehabilitation that can possibly be made available. I am glad to see this program advancing in this way, and I hope it will do a great deal for these people. But, Mr. Chairman, there is a very real gap to which the hon. member for Lanark has already referred, and I was sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare did not have something to say about that gap.
Just as I think it would not be the greatest kindness merely to provide a pension to an incapacitated person, if rehabilitation is possible and would be of real benefit to him, so I think it is an awful slap in the face to a person who is utterly incapable of being rehabilitated simply to say that there are these rehabilitation service grants, but no pension for such a person. In other words this program for the incapacitated people in our midst, for those who are permanent invalids, will not be complete until we have as part of our social security program a plan of pensions for these people.
Reference has been made by the minister and by the previous speaker to the debate that took place earlier this session on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Fort William. That is a debate we have had a good many times. We have had it on previous occasions on a motion put forward by the hon. member for Terrebonne, and other hon. members have put similar motions on the order paper. The support for a program of pensions for incapacitated persons for whom rehabilitation services mean nothing is, I am satisfied, very strong in all groups in this House of Commons, and I hope this gap will not remain very long. No doubt the very work that is done under this rehabilitation program, bringing to light, as it will, the 68108-297J
Supply-Health and Welfare number of people who cannot be rehabilitated, will prompt whatever government is in power the next little while to fill this gap with a program of pensions for incapacitated persons.
The third of the grants announced this afternoon by the minister is that known as laboratory and radiological grants, or in other words a grant for diagnostic services. I agree with the minister in the order in which he announced these three grants, and in the fact that he attached greatest importance to this third grant. There is no question but that it will be a great boon to medical practice in this country, a great boon to the health of our people generally, to have this money available for laboratory and radiological work and for improving diagnostic services and facilities. Here again I noted that the minister said the grant would be on a generally matching basis. Some time during the discussion perhaps he can tell us the difference between these two matching plans. He said that the child and maternal health grants would be on a dollar for dollar basis. He said that the laboratory and radiological grant would be on a generally matching basis. As I listened to him it did not seem to me there was much difference, and here again you have the matching principle being carried forward, whereas in my view we have altogether too much of that already in this country.
I am surprised at this government doing it, because while this government has been in power we have had the Rowell-Sirois investigation into federal-provincial relations and we have had the federal-provincial conference of 1945, in both of which there was brought out the desirability of making our country a unit, and trying to establish minimum standards' for Canadian welfare and wellbeing across the country without regard to the particular province in which a Canadian citizen happens to live.
One other thought occurs to me immediately when we learn of the introduction of the laboratory and radiological grant, and that is this. If we are now going to have-and highly welcome it is-better provisions for diagnosing diseases and ailments suffered by the Canadian people, it seems to me that is going to make more urgent than has been the case thus far the need for a program of health insurance. When I mention health insurance I have in mind in particular a plan to enable people to obtain and be able to pay for these services which, we are glad to note, are gradually being built up in this country.
And so just as my leader on May 14, 1948, on our behalf welcomed most heartily the health grants program announced at that time, and said that he hoped it would be looked upon as the foundation for a complete

Supply-Health and Welfare program including health insurance, so I make that same statement today. We are glad to have this announcement as to the extension of the health grants program to include these three services. But I suggest that it was singularly significant that, with the exception of one half sentence which the minister quoted from Mr. King, in which the words "health insurance" appeared, the minister never mentioned health insurance, on his own, in his entire speech this afternoon.

This afternoon the minister took occasion frequently to refer to the origin of this national health grants program in Mr. King's announcement of May 14, 1948. As I say, those of us who were here at that time remember that announcement very well. But I just wish to remind hon. members, and in particular the government, of the emphasis Mr. King placed upon the fact that in his view this was the beginning of a national health program, including health insurance. These health grants were to be the foundation for health insurance. In his very first sentence Mr. King said:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house on government policy with respect to health services and health insurance.
In the very next paragraph he refers to what had been the government's plan for a long time for a "nation-wide health program leading up to and ultimately including health insurance." As one goes on through his remarks he finds that Mr. King made reference repeatedly to health insurance as being the aim of the program being announced on

that date. For example, referring to hospital grants, he said:
Before health insurance can be established on an adequate basis, another development is essential.
And later on he said:
If, as the first stage in health insurance, hospital insurance were now to be introduced on a contributory basis, the demand that would arise for hospital accommodation simply could not be met.
Then he went on to point out that at that time there was an estimated shortage to the extent of 60,000 hospital beds. Later on he said, as the minister did this afternoon, that the five-year program envisaged the construction of hospital accommodation to the tune of 40,000 beds.
I was interested not only in hearing Mr. King's statement of May 14, 1948, and reading it again this evening, but I was also interested in the interpretation placed upon it by no less Liberal a newspaper than the Toronto Daily Star. I must confess I have shown this newspaper item in the house before, and I had not intended to drag it out again today. However, in view of what was said this afternoon I felt I should. This is the issue of the Toronto Daily Star for May 15, 1948, bearing on its front page a picture of Mr. King, three columns in width-and almost the full length of the page. This front page bears the heading "Can't Wait For Ontario- King". Then follows the subheading, "Delayed Health Plan As Long As We Could For Ontario-Mr. King".
Now that I have read the headings, I would ask hon. members to listen to one or two quotations which I think should be drawn to the attention of the house, in view of the minister's failure this afternoon to repeat- yes, even to do that-the assertions of the government in the past that it is aiming toward a program of health insurance. Listen to this, under the byline of Borden Spears:
National health insurance, the last feature in a complete social security program, is in sight for Canada as a result of the trail-blazing health grants announced yesterday by Prime Minister King.
And then, over on the other side of the page-because this is a full front-page spread -we have the interpretation of the day's news by another Star correspondent, Mr. Robert Taylor, who writes:
For the average man in Canada, the plans announced yesterday for the laying of the foundation of a national health insurance scheme means only that his national government has rolled up its sleeves, dug down in its pocket, and started a war on disease.
Then Mr. Taylor goes on in the article to quote what Mr. King had said in the house and out of the house, and also to quote what the Minister of National Health and Welfare

had said on that occasion. And then Mr. Robert Taylor goes on:
The government expects that within two years there will be operating in Canada at least part of the health insurance scheme.
This was in 1948.
Whom is my hon. friend quoting now?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Robert Taylor, after he had talked to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Is he quoting the Minister of National Health and Welfare?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No, not directly. He is interpreting what he took from Mr. King's statement of that day, according to the interview he had with the Prime Minister and with the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I am sure my hon. friend would agree with me that, estimable as Mr. Robert Taylor is as a reporter, that does not mean that he is a member of the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
A great many other people formed the same opinion Mr. Robert Taylor did, that Mr. King was to be taken at his word when he made his statement on May 14, 1948, that the health grants program was the foundation of a program of health insurance. And I suggest that Robert Taylor's interpretation was probably justified, not only by what Mr. King said in the House of Commons but also by his interviews with those in the government to whom he talked on that day.
I wish to continue reading that paragraph:
The government expects that within two years there will be operating in Canada at least part of the health insurance scheme. One suggestion is that hospital care might be the first thing provided, to be followed later on by medical care, then dental care for children in schools, and then for the whole population.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that not only does the expression "health insurance" appear-I did not count them, but I suppose at least ten or fifteen times-in the statement of Mr. King on May 14, 1948, but it has appeared in discussions on a national health program across the years, and in documents and speeches from this government.
As a matter of fact, the first reference to this matter in a Liberal document-at least, the first I know about which is official- was what was set out in the Liberal party platform of 1919, when they advocated a national program of health insurance. I have read again today the speeches from the throne in the early forties. Two or three references were made to health, and in every instance
Supply-Health and Welfare health insurance itself was mentioned. When I put the emphasis that I am putting on health insurance I have in mind the urgent need there is, not only for the facilities which are being built up in this country-I am glad they are being built up, and I pay a tribute to all those who have had any part in building them up-but that there be arrangements to enable the ordinary Canadian to pay for those services when he needs them. That is what Mr. King envisaged in health insurance for Canada; that is what the Liberal party has envisaged in health insurance across the years, at least in its pronouncements.
When you have health insurance mentioned in speeches from the throne from the early forties; when you have it mentioned in the Heagerty report; when you have it mentioned in the Marsh report; when you have it mentioned in the draft bill that was laid on the table of the house in August, 1944; when you have it mentioned repeatedly in the green book proposals by the federal government to the provinces in 1945; when you have it mentioned repeatedly in speeches of the present Minister of National Defence when he was minister of national health and welfare; when you have it mentioned many times in years gone by by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare, and then today you find no reference to it, unless he has found it-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

Supply-Health and Welfare I suggest that he go back and read his full statement on May 14, 1948, and get the point that Mr. King gave to this house, namely that he was then laying before us not only a health grants program, which was important for its immediate benefits, but a health grants program that was to be the foundation of a health insurance program for Canada.
This afternoon the minister found it possible to use the words "health insurance" only twice. I accept the correction that it was not once, that it was twice, but both times he was quoting the great authority to whom he refers. Not once did he even mention health insurance on his own.
As I say, across the years there have been these references to health insurance on the part of the government and on the part of the Liberal party as though they planned to do something along these lines. Mr. King in his statement, from which I have already quoted, referred to the need of getting hospitals constructed before you created a demand for them which would arise from a program of health insurance. The minister stood up this afternoon and boasted of the fact that the target of 40,000 beds in five years had been exceeded by 6,000. If that target has been exceeded it seems to me that "with the review after five years which Mr. King promised in 1948, and which the minister said this afternoon they were now undertaking, there should at least be a statement to the house as to where the government stands on this question of health insurance.
Across the years we have been voting money for health insurance studies. The research people in the minister's department have done an excellent job in this field. There have come to my desk from time to time-I have a number of them piled under my desk here now-some excellent memoranda and monographs on health insurance in eight or ten other countries in the world. I am sure the research people in the department were ready to give advice to the government or to a parliamentary committee, if we had had one when we were supposed to, in 1952, on this question of health insurance. But for some reason which the minister has not yet explained, in making the important statement he did this afternoon he based it on the important statement that Mr. King had made in 1948 and which laid the foundation for a health insurance program, but he did not even mention on his own part the words "health insurance." The words "health insurance" came out of his mouth twice, but only when he was quoting from Mr. King.
I need not take the time to repeat the history of this matter across the years. As a matter of fact I have already referred in


passing to the lip service the Liberals have given to health insurance beginning as far back as 1919, 34 years ago. Still we do not seem to be able to get this government to realize that with all the credit it has coming to it for what it has done to build up facilities for public health in this country, it has not yet tackled this problem of making it possible for people to afford the health care they need. That is what is involved in a health insurance program.
The last important statement the minister made about this was on June 6, 1952, during a similar debate on his estimates. I had had something to say about the fact that health insurance had been in the platform of the Liberal party since 1919 and that it had been confirmed by the party at its convention in 1948, and this is the reply the minister made on that occasion as reported on page 3007 of Hansard of that date:
There is no question where the party of which I am a member stands. We have advocated health insurance in our platforms as an objective. That was done, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, in the platform of 1919. It was mentioned in the platform of the convention at which the present Prime Minister was made the leader of this party. But that does not mean to say that because a party has a plank in its platform, it has got to be done overnight.
That is still my statement.

What a long night.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, what a long, long night; 34 years of night. The minister says it is still the objective of his party, but because his party has health insurance in its platform we should not expect it to be accomplished overnight.
The dawn is coming.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not know what sort of night the minister has had but he has even forgotten the words, and he did not tell the committee today what the government's plan is as to the relation between the health grants program and the eventual objective of health insurance, which I suppose they plan to achieve 34 years from now.
I said earlier that I did not want to detract by one iota from the praise the minister deserves for what he has done. But let it be understood that so far as the people of Canada are concerned, health facilities are but one plank in a national health program; they represent but one phase, and one of the most important of the others is health insurance to enable people to obtain these

facilities and pay for them when they need them, rather than being faced with bills or expenses that make it impossible for many people to get health services and which mortgage the lives of many others for years on end.
When we advocate a national health insurance program sometimes objections are raised. One objection is the usual one of cost. I have just two things to say on that. The special committee on old age security in 1950 pointed out that if we did have a national health insurance program the total cost would not be all new money, that much of it would be simply the rechannelling of money already being spent on health care.
The other thing I want to say is that the minister did not seem to be worried about the dollars involved in the program he presented to this house. I am glad he did not. He simply stands up and says, if I can remember some of the things he said this afternoon, that you cannot measure these things in dollars and cents, that the health of the nation is extremely important, that it is the greatest thing a government can do for its people. I think that is a good attitude, and if the minister takes that attitude toward the money that must be spent on the health grants program I simply ask him to take the same attitude toward a health insurance program to spread the cost of health and medical care more evenly over the population.
In that connection I shall not take the time to put these statements on the record again, because I have done so several times, last year on the 5th and 6th of June and also in other years, but there are no better statements of the need for health insurance, its validity and its common sense, than have come from the government itself in some of its own documents, notably the green book proposals of the government of Canada to-
