speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
As I say, Mr. Chairman, no better statements of the common sense and the validity of health insurance have been made than those we have been given in documents and in words by this government. But apparently health insurance has been forgotten by this government, if we are to judge by the kind of speech the minister made this afternoon.
Supply-Health and Welfare
I have said that a national health program requires facilities, and I congratulate the government upon what they have done. But it also requires health insurance arrangements to pay for the medical care about which I have been talking, and it also requires a program of sickness benefits. I shall not take time now to go into that because there will be other opportunities, but I wanted to include it along with these other two as being the three important aspects of an over-all national health program.
I have said several times during the course of my remarks that I give the minister and the federal government all the praise they have coming to them for what they have accomplished in providing health facilities, but like the hon. member for Lanark I could not help but feel that when the minister was speaking this afternoon he might have given a little more praise to the provinces and the municipalities which have also played an important part in this program. I give him credit for digressing at one point from what appeared to be a manuscript to bring in a reference to the provinces. But let it be remembered that a great deal of the pioneering in public health in this country has been carried on by the provinces; and when you are talking about the increase in hospital beds, when you are talking about the development of cancer research, of diagnostic services and free medical care of one kind and another, let it not be forgotten that a great deal of the credit should go to the various provinces of Canada.
Indeed, there is much credit to be given to the municipalities. I think of what my own city of Winnipeg has done by way of pioneering in this field. We have nothing to lose, either as different parties or as different jurisdictions in this country, in giving credit where credit is due. This is a great national effort in which we are engaged. We are all concerned for the health of the people of the country, and I hope we will show that concern by welcoming, as we do, slight steps forward such as those which were announced today. But let us not stop there; let us go on and achieve the full program that Mr. King talked about in his announcement of May 14, 1948, a program which we believe the people of this country expect and which Canada today, with her great expanding economy, can well afford. Indeed, an adequate health program is some-think we cannot afford not to have.
There are other items that come under the minister's department about which I wish to have something to say, but I shall leave any details with respect to them to a later occasion, because I am glad to join with the minister and the hon. member for Lanark in putting the primary emphasis at this stage

Supply-Health and Welfare of the debate on the health situation so far as our people are concerned. When the time comes I shall have something to say about our social security program, about the need for further improvements in our old age pension legislation, about the need for doing something with respect to the means test on the blindness allowance and the amount of the blindness allowance. Indeed, there are a good many places in Canada's program of social security where there is room for tremendous improvement, and as the minister knows I shall continue to urge these improvements.

Mr. Chairman, realizing as I do that there are some 38 individual items in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and realizing that we shall have an opportunity to discuss specific items under these appropriations it is not my intention to go beyond the statement made to the house by the minister this afternoon.
Possibly I should make reference in passing to the government's remarkable sense of timing, possibly the minister's remarkable sense of timing. Prior to the election in 1945 it was indicated to us that family allowances would become the order of the day. In 1948, prior to the 1949 election, it was indicated that a rather extensive scheme of health services involving health grants would become operative. Now in 1953, just prior to an election, we are advised of the making of grants in three new fields. That indicates a rather remarkable sense of timing. As I have said in the house more than once probably elections should take place more frequently.
However, in saying that I would not want it thought, even though I may hold these views with respect to timing, that I am opposed to the proposed grants. I would not want it to be thought that in saying these things I am at the same time opposed to the grants outlined by the minister this afternoon. On May 14, 1948, when the late prime minister announced the new scheme of grants for national health services, my leader, the hon. member for Peace River, made a few brief observations. Hon. members who were here at that time will recall that the leaders of the opposition parties were not given much notice of the statement, and therefore their first observations were quite brief. As found at page 3937 of Hansard for May 14, 1948, the hon. member for Peace River opened his remarks with this observation:
I do not believe that the Prime Minister could leave a better monument to the long years of service he has given to this country as leader of


th'e Liberal party than the foundations of a progressive health security program. I listened with close attention to the announcement he made, and I certainly want to congratulate the government on the step they have taken.
Later the hon. member said:
We were particularly pleased this afternoon to see the government take some action against these scourges of the human race which, if they are allowed to run their, course, are likely to impoverish whole families-tuberculosis, cancer and similar diseases. This is a splendid start in that direction.
He concluded his observations with these remarks:
We look upon this proposal only as a step forward, and I am sure that is what the Prime Minister had in mind-that it would be the foundation for a program of health security which I hope in the years to come will grow into the much more comprehensive scheme the Prime Minister must have envisioned.
Therefore it can be clearly taken from these observations of that date that we supported the proposals set forth by the late prime minister when he made his announcement upon that occasion. We are able to say again today that we are pleased to note that a forward step is being taken with respect to meeting the problems which confront Canadian people in this field of health. However, I must point out at this time that for many years I have heard this reference to health insurance and I have come to the conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that health insurance means different things to different people. I am inclined to believe that the time has come when, if we are going to debate health insurance, we should have specific proposals before us.
Some persons look upon health insurance as being state medicine. Well, there is a form of health insurance which I would classify as state medicine. It is that type of health insurance that I am personally convinced involves regimentation, red tape and a number of other most undesirable characteristics. Personally I would be opposed to that type of health insurance. If by health insurance one means a health program in which the federal government, the provincial government and the municipal governments along with the people themselves work co-operatively toward the highest possible standard of health service, then I would experience no difficulty in going along with that proposition. Perhaps that is what certain persons mean when they talk of health insurance, but perhaps they mean something else.
So I say the time has come when a definite and comprehensive scheme of health insurance should be set before us by those who advocate it. I would appreciate that, in

order that I might deal with a specific proposition. I realize that health insurance is in effect in many countries, but there is a vast difference between any two schemes which one might wish to use as exhibits. I find myself very confused with respect to all of them. I am certain that in 1948 when the prime minister of Canada referred to health insurance, he did not have in mind the same thing that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has in his mind. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre urges a scheme of health insurance. The government says and has said that it believes in a scheme of health insurance, but I am sure the two are miles apart. Therefore I repeat what I said, that I would like to have a specific proposal in regard to health insurance before I would be prepared to commit myself with respect to it.
This afternoon, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Health and Welfare quoted a reference by a one-time British prime minister-and I do not recall the exact words used by the minister today-to the effect that the health of our people is our greatest asset. We have used that expression time and again because we are absolutely convinced that it is a fact. We were rather pleased to hear the minister say certain things this afternoon, and I for one hope that the meaning that I took out of certain of his declarations were the meanings he had in mind when he uttered them. For example, he said that in any proposal that is brought forward we must not destroy the patient-doctor relationship. I agree with that absolutely, Mr. Chairman. I never want to see our medical service in this country put on a production line basis, the same as automobiles running along the production line in the course of manufacture.
Hear, hear.

I am convinced from personal experience that if we set about to dehumanize medicine-and that is exactly what we would be doing under state medicine-we would destroy the basic and fundamental value of it. I hold very strong feelings in that respect, Mr. Chairman. I think of my own relationships with my own doctor, for example. He knows the family background; he knows the background of my youngsters; he knows the psychological implications; and, as is true of every family doctor, he realizes the exaggerations or distortions that a patient may exhibit.
I think it is imperative, Mr. Chairman, that we maintain the doctor-patient relationship in any scheme. The minister said this afternoon that he did not want to see centralization under any scheme. I think that was
Supply-Health and Welfare his reference, because I made a note about it. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, I agree with him there. I think the finest arrangement that can be made is for the federal government to make grants to the provinces and for the provinces to work in co-operation with the municipalities in the administration of those moneys along with their own. It is on that local level that the problem is best known and best understood. It is on that basis that we are able to render the type of service which is in the best interests of our people.
When the minister said we should not destroy the patient-doctor relationship, I believe he also went so far as to indicate that we did not want to regiment patients, doctors or nurses in hospitals; and I agree. I mention these things, Mr. Chairman, because in my conception of a desirable program, whether you want to call it a health insurance program or just a health program, I think these basic and fundamental principles are essential and must be preserved.
Before I refer to the three separate types of grants with which the minister made the house familiar this afternoon, may I say a word about another matter. The grants made to assist the provinces and municipalities to construct or enlarge hospitals have played a most valuable part. Let us remember, _ however, that the provinces and the municipalities in many cases had gone quite some distance in the field prior to grants being made to assist them. That, however, does not at all detract from the fact that in all provinces in Canada hospitals have been constructed which those provinces would not have had except for these grants.
A problem arises in connection with the matter, as I think it arises in connection with all grants which are made to the provinces on a dollar for dollar basis. When you make such grants to a province you are saying, as two previous speakers have already indicated, that if the provinces are in the position where they have the money to match the grant dollar for dollar, the result is that they may take advantage of the grants.
Now, that is fine when the province has the financial resources to match these grants from the federal government. What I would suggest is that we continue such grants on that basis, but that we also make additional grants taking into account the weighted factor. When you make grants on a dollar for dollar basis you are not providing an opportunity for the people right across the country to enjoy the same level of health services. You are saying to the province which may be economically unfortunate that

Supply-Health and Welfare the people of that province are going to continue to experience less in the way of health services than do the people in another part of Canada. If in addition to these grants we made further payments on a weighted basis to help those who are not so well able to help themselves, then I think probably we would be going much further toward the solution of the problem which confronts us.
Today the minister said grants were being made for child and maternal health services. I think it was quite important that the minister put that first, because I believe it is a field in which a lot of good can be accomplished. I hope the minister and the house will pardon me if I make a personal reference, and I do not do so in any partisan sense at all. I well recall that we in Alberta had an infant mortality rate which was not pleasant to behold. We inaugurated a scheme whereby we provided so-called free hospitalization. It does not cost the patient anything except what would be paid in the course of the usual property taxes.
Under this plan the expectant mother enters the hospital and is allowed to stay there for twelve days without making any direct payment. If the mother is unable or does not desire to enter hospital, a straight grant of $40 is made to her. I understand that, although this has not been a factor in the past, provision is being made to grant up to 50 per cent of the cost of extras, that is right across the board so far as hospitalization is concerned. Hand in hand with that is what the minister referred to this afternoon as the health units, in which we have our district health nurses. The nurses arrange for holding pre-natal and post-natal clinics, and so on.
The result of this program has been a remarkable downward movement in our infant mortality index. I cannot give the figures offhand, but the result has been outstanding. In other words there is not the slightest excuse for a baby being born outside of a hospital. My leader has just informed me that the scheme has been in operation since 1944, and we have had an excellent opportunity to see how it works. When the minister indicates to us that grants are being made to the provinces for the establishment of clinics for educational services for expectant mothers and for educational services-I presume that would be the appropriate expression-after the birth of a child, then I can envision a remarkable improvement in that whole general field of infant and mother welfare. I think this is a splendid thing.
I took some exception, of course, to the minister's method of indicating-perhaps it was an inference and perhaps he did not mean it at all, I do not know-that 10,000 infant

lives had been saved as a consequence of federal government grants of one kind or another. We are prepared to share the credit with him, but we feel that the provinces and municipalities have done much. I do not want to exclude the voluntary organizations when I refer to the provinces, the federal government and the municipalities. I think that in combination they have all done much to effect this improved condition so far as infants and their mothers are concerned.
This afternoon the minister referred to rehabilitation services for the incapacitated, the handicapped. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, that is a field wherein much good can be accomplished. But I must agree with previous speakers who indicated that there is a necessity for help by way of pensions for those persons who are permanently incapacitated. Two provinces in Canada have already provided pensions for such persons. I believe Ontario has done so for some time, I do not know how long, and Alberta is now inaugurating a program providing such pensions. I realize the burden that could well fall upon the shoulders of some of our provinces if they were to undertake similar programs. I am not criticizing them for not having done so. Far be it from me to do that. They are in a better position than I am to realize what their financial resources are. It does, however, put us in a rather peculiar position in Canada when we say that in two provinces the incapacitated get pensions but in the other eight provinces they do not. I am excluding the veteran from this, because I am talking of the civilian.
I believe that, along with rehabilitation services, along with vocational training, the federal government and the provincial governments should try to create an arrangement under which the permanently incapacitated persons of this country may receive pensions. It is a rather tragic experience for any member of parliament to be approached by a civilian who is physically incapacitated. He does not qualify for anything but municipal relief. In a great country like this it hurts one to have to tell the man, who possibly has lived in the country for 50 or 60 years and has done much towards developing it, that because of something over which he has had no control and as a result of which he has lost the financial resources he did have, he must seek municipal relief. I suggest that it should not be too long before none of us, as members of parliament, is faced with the necessity of telling an individual that his only hope is municipal relief.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the third aspect of the program is the extension of laboratory and diagnostic services. We feel that this is a field in which inestimable good can be

accomplished. I feel, however, that conceivably some provinces might not be able to take advantage of the full program, although I do understand there are grants to be made that do not have to be matched.
On behalf of my colleagues I might indicate to the minister that we support these new grants. We feel that that one element of change in the grants should be introduced to take cognizance of the weighted factor so we could take care of the situation in all parts of Canada. In this way we could bring about greater equality of health services.
I desire to pay tribute to those who have been striving valiantly to provide us with health services. I am speaking particularly of the doctors. I know they are criticized, but all of us are criticized, and most unfairly in many respects. I think the minister hit the nail on the head today when he said that many doctors do not go into the more outlying points because of the lack of facilities. They are trained to use modern facilities.
I know this program is going to assist many of our smaller hospitals to procure certain of those facilities. I pay tribute to the medical men of our country and to our nurses, many of whom are overworked today because of the shortage of nurses, and those who are administering our hospitals, and so forth. Too frequently we criticize, but on the other hand a great deal of credit is due them, Mr. Chairman.
In conclusion I should like to emphasize one thing. When it comes to this question of health insurance I realize there is an argument about the word "insurance". Someone will say that it involves certain specific things. We have reached a stage in this old world where we use words pretty loosely, but I favour a scheme wherein we take advantage of existing facilities. We expand those facilities. We keep administration on the local levels; we do not have regimentation; we maintain the greatest degree of freedom which it is possible to maintain. It is going to take a bit of time, but I think one would have to be viewing things with his eyes closed if he were not to see that we have made good progress.
Possibly we have not moved as fast as some people would like to see us move, but in our municipalities, in our provinces and federally we have made a good deal of progress in recent years. I hope we shall move along as rapidly as we can, providing the essential facilities and the personnel, and always have as our objective the best interests of all our Canadian people.

I shall be brief. While excellent work has been done in recent
Supply-Health and Welfare years in the province of Alberta, I think it would be only fair to recall to the committee tonight the service rendered to that province and to Canada by the late Hon. Alexander G. MacKay, who was the first minister of health in Alberta. He was a pioneer in bringing in legislation of the kind which has been presented by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Since I come from a place far removed from the cities, I know of the excellent work which is being done by doctors on the frontiers of this country, where they work without the facilities that are available in the larger centres, and where they render tremendous service to settlers, miners and trappers in distant places. But I should like to commend the minister for the very progressive step that he has taken; well-timed-of course, well-timed. The secret of his great success and that of our late prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, was the ability to time these things properly and then to see that they were carried out promptly.

Mr. Chairman, like the other hon. members who have spoken, I was very glad to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare mention the health grants the government is going to bring in. I think they are a good thing, of course.
As one who has been pressing the government for a couple of years now to do something in the way of rehabilitation, I am glad to see that at least a start is being made. I hope the government will extend this program to a large extent, because the results that have been achieved in the United States in this regard have proved that money spent on rehabilitation is not charity or money poured down the drain; it is the best investment the government can possibly make from the point of view of cash return on what it puis in, as well as the great improvement in the health standard of the people.
I was very surprised, just as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and other hon. members who have spoken have been surprised, that the minister did not make more reference to the vital problem of health insurance. I was also surprised to note that the only two statements he did make were not his own but very brief references to statements made by his former leader, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You had better read my speech tomorrow.

I have read it. The minister made two very brief references to health insurance, and both of them were in references to what Mr. King said. If I am wrong

Supply-Health and Welfare then I will certainly admit it tomorrow after I read his remarks, but I read them over very carefully and that is all I could find in them.
I sincerely wish the minister would start making statements about health insurance on his own. After all, he has been the minister for quite a while now; he should know his own mind. He has made a study of it, and if he has not, he certainly should have done so. After all, Mr. King's statements are five years old, and this is a very critical problem to a vast number of Canadians, I would say to all Canadians. I am surprised that by now the minister has not called together a conference of provincial health ministers and representatives of the medical profession to talk over the question of health insurance. It is the only way the government can know what kind of plan is the best. I feel that the provincial health ministers are very anxious to meet with the Minister of National Health and Welfare to discuss this problem.
We confer constantly; we have done it twice this year.

There is one provincial minister of health who does not think the minister and he confer together nearly often enough on this problem, and that is the Hon. Mackinnon Phillips, minister of health of Ontario.
I speak from personal knowledge, because I spent several hours with him recently talking about this very problem. Perhaps the minister read a statement that Mr. Mackinnon Phillips made in Toronto on April 20, last, as reported in the Toronto Telegram. The statement is headed: "Health Chief Wants Confab on Insurance" and reads as follows:
Ontario health minister Mackinnon Phillips today approved the idea of a conference of all provinces' health ministers to talk over the possibilities of a national health insurance scheme.
Dr. Phillips felt it was time such a scheme was investigated in detail.
Dr. Phillips does not want this government to jam down the throat of Ontario, or of any province, some scheme that it may conjure up in its own mind. He feels, as I am sure all the other provincial health ministers feel, that this thing can be worked out only by lengthy conferences of all the provincial ministers, the representatives of the medical profession, the dental profession, the hospitals, and so on. Surely the minister realizes that, and it is long overdue. This conference should have been called together and started on its way.
I have talked to many ordinary people who would be benefited by a health insurance plan; I have talked to a lot of doctors; I have talked to a lot of insurance men. I am very interested

in this thing and I have spoken to many people about it; and I am convinced that the people of this country do not want a state medicine plan. They feel that it is cumbersome; it is costly; it destroys the doctor-patient relationship which they have learned to value very highly.
Doctors are in favour of health insurance of the right kind, because it will help them to collect their bills for services rendered. They do not want to be put into the strait-jacket of a state medicine plan, and that is why they are very anxious to get together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare and talk this thing over in great detail.
Is my hon. friend aware that such meetings take place almost constantly; that we had a meeting of that kind with the Canadian Medical Association about five weeks ago?

Does the minister not think it would be a courtesy on his part to advise the health minister, for instance, of Ontario, of that fact, and perhaps ask him to sit in and talk over this most important matter?
Is my hon. friend not aware that twice a year federal and provincial government officials meet here in Ottawa for at least two days, and that they met here about seven weeks ago?
I say that I talked at great length with the minister of health of Ontario, and according to him the minister has not discussed this matter with the provincial ministers of health.

Will my hon. friend permit me to say that I am quite sure the minister of health of Ontario, for whom I have great respect and with whom I have great collaboration and co-operation, never made that statement.

Mr. Chairman, I spoke to him for two hours not more than two weeks ago, and it was very clear to me that this subject has not been discussed in any worth-while manner between the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the provincial minister. That is why he feels there should be a conference, and that this matter should be discussed properly and thoroughly and a plan worked out which could be proceeded with.
The minister said last year, when we discussed this matter at length, that we could not proceed with health insurance because we did not have the equipment to handle it. Well, how in the world does the minister know whether we have or have not the equipment needed to handle it until
he has some idea of the kind of plan this equipment would be required to handle?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Is not my hon. friend aware that we have completed a sickness survey, that we have also just had a survey of all provincial health services? And, incidentally, the province of Ontario did not make a recommendation along the lines my hon. friend is now advocating.
The sickness survey to which the minister refers is, I understand, the provincial health survey.
No. It is a national sickness survey; we discussed it here for about two days last year.

The Minister of National Health
and Welfare has not sat down and talked over the question of a national health insurance plan with the representatives of the provincial governments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite wrong when he says that.
The minister had better get it straight.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You had better get it straight.

If the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been talking this matter over in some detail with the minister of health in Ontario, then certainly he has made very little impression upon that gentleman. If the minister says there have been some conversations, then the minister in Ontario should be in possession of some information on the matter. I say to the minister here tonight that he is completely wrong in that respect because, as I have pointed out, I have just talked with the Hon. Mackinnon Phillips, minister of health in Ontario, only about two weeks ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Come and see me after we adjourn.

Oh, I would rather talk the matter over right here. It is all very friendly, and we are not far apart. I am very interested in talking to my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and I like to have his comments on the record, too. I am hopeful, of course, that at some time we are going to be able to pin down our Minister of National Health and Welfare as to what his feelings are about health insurance. The government has been promising it for 34 years; and every time there is an election, Liberal candidates all over the country say, "Vote us in, and you will get health insurance." Then after the election is over absolutely nothing happens.
I think it is about time this government started to get honest with the people of
Supply-Health and Welfare
Canada. After promising health insurance since 1919, it should start to do something concrete by bringing in a plan of health insurance, or at least by laying the foundations for one. The government should get together with the provincial ministers and their representatives with a view to deciding the kind of plan that would be desirable and practicable. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has not conveyed that information to the provincial ministers of health as of this date.

I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but I do say he is in error, and I do not know how many times I have to tell him. Let me repeat that there is continual collaboration in this matter not only with the minister of health in Ontario, but I have discussed the matter with the hon. gentleman's provincial chief, the premier of the province, Hon. Mr. Frost. I can only say that when my hon. friend becomes my parliamentary assistant perhaps he will be able to speak more authoritatively as to what I have really done.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the
Minister of National Health and Welfare has talked to the minister of health in Ontario, but perhaps the minister of health in Ontario has the same difficulty with the minister that we have here in the House of Commons, because I know the minister in Ontario has not been able to find out what is in the mind of our Minister of National Health and Welfare.
He thinks I am a good guy.

I am sure the minister in Ontario has no idea whether the federal minister is for or against health insurance; what he likes or what he does not like. They may have been talking together for some time; but, just as in our conversations here in the House of Commons, no one knows any more about health insurance at the end of our long discussions than he knew before we began. That is because the Minister of National Health and Welfare is about as easy to pin down to a statement as it is to pin a piece of jelly to the wall. One is just about as easy as the other.
There are a number of rumours flying around, and I wonder if the minister would settle them right now. These rumours are to the effect that the government intends to bring in a measure of health insurance by order in council between the time parliament closes and the date of the election. Would the minister please give me a yes or no answer on that question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend is quite concerned about his next election, otherwise

Supply-Health and Welfare he would not be so apprehensive. However, he must know that this government, in respect to other governments he has supported, is not an order in council government.

Oh, oh. I guess the minister did not read Hansard setting out the recent debate in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce was concerned. That was regarding a small matter of shipping to China. I repeat this question: Does the government intend to introduce a measure of health insurance between the time parliament closes and the date of the election-yes or no?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have such high esteem for my hon. friend that I can hardly credit that a man trained in our universities, as he is, and who now serves in our parliamentary system, does not yet know the limitations on the executive arm of government in this country, and under our constitution.

I think it is obvious, Mr. Chairman, why the Hon. Mackinnon Phillips knows nothing about what is in the minister's mind, because I am wondering if the minister does himself. Everyone in this parliament knows very well there are no limits to what this government can do, if it wishes. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, "If we want to get away with it, who will stop us?" And if this government can bring in an order in council, as it did a week ago, when parliament was sitting, in connection with the simple matter of sending ships to China, then of course it can bring in a measure of health insurance after parliament closes and before the date of the next election. It can do it in exactly the same way it brought in a wide measure of tax reduction only a few days before the 1945 election.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Come to my room after this sitting, and I will take you into my confidence.

No, I want to know now. Either the minister does intend or he does not intend to bring in a measure of health insurance after the session ends, and as an election measure. And as the minister does not deny it, we must conclude he is going to do just that. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, sitting over there, simply smiled when reference was made to the fact that we must believe in Santa Claus, implying that the government believes in Santa Claus, and that they intend to bring in health insurance before the election date so as to lure votes into the ballot boxes, as they have done in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question?

Yes.
[Mr. Martin.!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Does my hon. friend really say he does not believe in Santa Claus?

Of course I believe in Santa Claus. And, as the minister knows, I have been urging this government for the last two or three years to do something about health insurance; I have been urging him, and urging him, and urging him. Now, I take it, the government does intend-the minister does not deny it-to hold out another evergreen election lure in the form of health insurance, at the time of the next election. If the minister does not deny it we can only assume that that is the government's intention. There is nothing to stop them if they want to do it, and they certainly can do it by order in council. They have done this sort of thing over and over again.
So I take it we are going to have national health insurance introduced by this government by order in council between now and the election date. And, now that we know that, we can understand clearly why the minister has not called together a conference of provincial ministers. He does not want his plan to be known ahead of time; he does not want it to be interfered with. All he wants is to state: This is the plan; this is what we are going to do for you electors. Now go to the polls and vote for us again, and we will promise to bring it in after the next election.
But they have been doing that for 34 years and of course it does not mean any more today than it did in the past, so I am sure the public will not take it too seriously. It is nice to know anyway, at long last, what the government does intend to do about health insurance.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know if the minister will be able to pay much attention to me after having been elevated to the heights of confusion by the previous speaker. The hon. member has spoken tonight with as much authority on health insurance and social welfare as he spoke on housing in Saint John a few days ago. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a problem in connection with civil defence affecting my own particular area.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Could not the hon. member find it more convenient to deal with that when we come to the particular item?

It may be that I shall have to be elsewhere as these items continue, and I should like to speak for a few minutes this evening. For some time now Saint John has been extremely interested in civil defence, because our city and the surrounding area are considered to be a prime bombing target

in the event of hostilities. A considerable amount of money has been spent to date by the municipality in order to co-operate with the Department of National Health and Welfare in providing proper facilities for the defence of the area and to take care of emergencies should they develop.
The city has already spent something like $10,000 in this regard. I might say here that the city of Saint John and Saint John county are most grateful for the generous co-operation of the minister through his officers in that particular section of his department, for the training of instructors in civil defence as well as aid by way of equipment. To date this has been worth approximately $18,000.
I understand that the department through the director of civil defence has made an offer to the province of New Brunswick whereby that province could obtain more money from the federal department by putting up a like amount. Up to date the province of New Brunswick has not agreed to accept that very generous offer on the part of the department and thus be able to implement a sound system of civil defence in those areas of the province where it is considered vital that we should have such a system.
I understand that two alternative offers were made. One was that the province could put up dollar for dollar with the department, and the other was that a municipality could put up one-third, the province one-third and the federal government the remaining one-third. Up to date the city of Saint John has not been able to enter into this arrangement because the provincial government has not agreed to put up the $46,000, I believe it is- I may be slightly off, but it would be only a matter of a few dollars-either by matching the federal government dollar by dollar or by agreeing to put up one-third, so that the city and county of Saint John can put up the other one-third and thus be able to derive further benefits from the national civil defence program.
Many of the citizens of Saint John are extremely concerned about this. I am going to ask the minister if he cannot deviate from the hard and fast policy. Even though the province of New Brunswick will not agree to put up the money to enable us to get more support from his department for civil defence in our area, perhaps some arrangement could be made whereby the city of Saint John could match an amount to be put up by the department and thus carry on our civil defence program.
There are many hundreds of people who are prepared to go forward with this program on a voluntary basis. There is the Red Cross
Supply-Health and Welfare and the St. John Ambulance; and we have 25 instructors who have been trained in civil defence here in Ottawa at the cost of a good many thousands of dollars. We do not want this program to collapse; therefore I am asking the minister if some other means cannot be devised whereby our municipality can come in under this program without the assistance of the province.
I thank the minister for being so tolerant as to allow me to speak perhaps somewhat irregularly.

My conscience would not rest over the week end if I did not have a chance to say some of the nice things I have in mind about the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I am sure he would like to have me say those things, but under the circumstances perhaps he will not mind my putting them over until Monday morning when I can do it at greater length than I could tonight, the hands of the clock being in their present position.

To authorize and provide for the operation of a revolving fund in accordance with the provisions of section 58 of the Financial Administration Act, for the purposes of financing the production of improved and new varieties of seeds, including administrative expenses, and the acquiring of livestock for experimental purposes; the amount to be charged to the revolving fund at any one time not to exceed $620,000, of which $250,000 has already been provided under vote 556, Appropriation Act, No. 4, 1952, $370,000.
